senses.definition: The method by which a device performs its function.
The method or practice by which actions are done.
The act or process of operating (verb): agency; the exertion of power, physical, mechanical, or moral.
A planned undertaking.
A business or organization.
A surgical procedure.
A procedure for generating a value from one or more other values (the operands).
A function which maps zero or more (but typically two) operands to a single output value.
A military campaign (e.g. Operation Desert Storm).
Effect produced; influence.

The doctor contemplated the difficult operation.
Doctors refused to perform a second operation.

examples.translation: 自從手術後，我父親一直處於良好的狀態。

etymology.text: From Middle English operacioun, from Old French operacion, from Latin operātiō, from the verb operor (“to work”), from opus, operis (“work”). Equivalent to operate + -ion.

Any great sin or wickedness; iniquity.
Criminal acts collectively.
The habit or practice of committing crimes.
That which occasions crime.

examples.translation: 他們原諒了他的罪行。

examples.text: Blasphemy is a victimless crime.

examples.text: I am not connected to this crime in any way.
examples.translation: 我與這起犯罪沒有任何關係。

examples.text: He ought to be punished if he commits a crime.
examples.translation: 如果他犯了罪，他應該受到懲罰。

etymology.text: From Middle English cryme, crime, from Old French crime, crimne, from Latin crīmen. Displaced native Old English firen.

senses.definition: A specialized division of a university.
An institution of higher education teaching undergraduates.
A university.
A postsecondary institution that offers vocational training and/or associate's degrees.
A non-specialized, semi-autonomous division of a university, with its own faculty, departments, library, etc.
An institution of further education at an intermediate level; sixth form.
An institution for adult education at a basic or intermediate level (teaching those of any age).
A high school or secondary school.
A residential hall associated with a university, possibly having its own tutors.
A government high school, short for junior college.
A group of people sharing common purposes or goals, especially ecclesiastics or professionals; a corporate group; a group of colleagues.
An electoral college.
A private (non-government) primary or high school.
A bilingual school.

examples.text: My sister became a college student.

examples.translation: 他在大學修讀歷史。

examples.text: My brother seems to enjoy himself at college.
examples.translation: 我弟弟似乎在大學過得很愉快。

etymology.text: From Middle English college, from Middle French college, from Old French college, from Latin collēgium. Doublet of collegium.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語（college），來自中古法語與古法語（college），再源自拉丁語（collēgium）。與（collegium）為雙式詞。

senses.definition: One who belongs to a group.
Part of an animal capable of performing a distinct office; an organ; a limb.
A function or piece of data associated with each separate instance of a class.
A part of a whole.
The penis.
One of the propositions making up a syllogism.
An element of a set.
the judge or adjudicator in a consumer court.
A part of a discourse or of a period, sentence, or verse; a clause.
Either of the two parts of an algebraic equation, connected by the equality sign.
A file stored within an archive file.

etymology.text: From Middle English membre, from Old French membre, from Latin membrum (“limb, body part”), from Proto-Italic *memzrom, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms, *mēms-rom (“flesh”). Akin to Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌼𐌶 (mimz, “meat, flesh”), Crimean Gothic menus.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語（membre），來自古法語（membre），再源自拉丁語（membrum）「肢體、身體部位」，最終來自原始印歐語（*mḗms）「肉」。與哥德語（mimz）「肉」同源。

senses.definition: A committee that leads or governs (e.g. city council, student council).
A local authority.
Discussion or deliberation.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English counseil (“meeting, conference, commune”), from Old French conseil (“advice, deliberation, thought”), from Latin cōnsilium (“plan, intention, design, purpose”), from cōnsulō (“consult, seek counsel from, take counsel from, deliberate, reflect”), from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁- (“take, grab”).

senses.definition: Any goods which are illicit or illegal to possess.
Goods which are prohibited from being traded, smuggled goods.
A black slave during the American Civil War who had escaped to, or been captured by, Union forces.

examples.text: Contraband may be confiscated.
examples.translation: 違禁品可能被沒收。

examples.text: This is contraband.
examples.translation: 這就是違禁品。

examples.text: Examples in smuggling include suitcases with false bottoms for hiding contraband.

etymology.text: From Spanish contrabanda (modern spelling contrabando), from Italian contrabando (modern spelling contrabbando), from contra (“against”) + bando (“ban”), and reinforced by French contrebande.
etymology.native: 「contrabanda」源自西班牙語，由義大利語「contrabando」演化而來，意為「對抗禁令」，由「contra」（對抗）與「bando」（禁令）組成，並受法語「contrebande」影響。

senses.definition: Goods which are or were offered or intended for sale.
Commercial goods connected (branded) with an entity such as a team, band, company, charity, work of fiction, festival, or meme. (Commonly shortened to merch.)
A commodity offered for sale; an article of commerce; a kind of merchandise.
The act or business of trading; trade; traffic.

examples.text: This merchandise isn't sold in Japan.

Please don't touch the merchandise.

etymology.text: From Middle English marchaundise (“commerce, trading; buying; business transaction, deal; merchandise, goods, wares; possessions”), from Anglo-Norman marchaundise and Old French marcheandise (modern French marchandise), from Old French marcheant (“seller, vendor”) (ultimately from Latin mercātus (“buying and selling, trade, traffic; market; marketplace”), possibly originally Etruscan) + -ise (suffix forming feminine nouns, often denoting a quality or state). The English word is analysable as mer

senses.definition: A serious criminal offense, which, under United States federal law, is punishable by a term of imprisonment of not less than one year or by the death penalty in the most serious offenses.

relations.native: 牆壁、要塞或堤防因破壞而形成的缺口；固體物體因暴力破裂產生的空間

etymology.text: From Middle English felony, felonie, from Old French felonie (“evil, immoral deed”), from felon (“evildoer”). Ultimately of Proto-Germanic origin. More at felon. By surface analysis, felon + -y.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語 felonie，來自舊法語 felonie（惡行），再來自 felon（作惡者）。最終源於原始日耳曼語。詳見 felon。從字面分析為 felon 加上 -y 詞尾。

To bring in surreptitiously
To thrash or be thrashed by a bear's claws, or to swipe at or be swiped at by a person's arms in a bearlike manner.
senses.native: 被熊爪抓傷，或以人臂如熊般揮打或被揮打

senses.definition: To fondle or cuddle.

examples.text: They smuggled him to Algeria.
examples.translation: 他們將他暗中帶到阿爾及利亞。

examples.translation: 警察以走私為由逮捕了他。

examples.text: He smuggled something into Australia for her.

etymology.text: From earlier smuckle, either from Dutch smokkelen (“to smuggle”), a frequentative form of Middle Dutch smūken (“to act secretly, be sneaky”), from Old Dutch *smugan, or from Dutch Low Saxon or German Low German smuggeln; all are from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to creep; slip through or into”).
etymology.native: 源於早期的 smuckle，來自荷蘭語 smokkelen（走私），或源自荷蘭低地德語 smuggeln；皆源於原始西日耳曼語 *smeugan（爬行、溜進）。

senses.definition: Young; not fully developed.
Characteristic of youth or immaturity; childish.

examples.text: Juvenile delinquency is increasing.
examples.translation: 青少年犯罪數量正在增加。

examples.text: Tom is a juvenile delinquent.
examples.translation: 湯姆是一名青少年罪犯。

examples.text: The juvenile crimes are increasing recently.
examples.translation: 最近青少年犯罪案件數量持續上升。

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin iuvenīlis (“youthful; juvenile”), from iuvenis (“young; a youth”) + -īlis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a relationship or a pertaining to). Iuvenis is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”), from *h₂óyu (“long life; lifetime”) (from *h₂ey- (“age; life”)) + *h₁én (“in”).
etymology.native: 借自拉丁語 iuvenīlis（意為「青春的；少年的」），由 iuvenis（意為「年輕的；青年」）+ -īlis（構成形容詞的後綴，表示與某事物相關）組成。iuvenis 最終源自原始印歐語 *h₂yuh₁en-（意為「年輕的」），來自 *h₂óyu（意為「長壽；一生」）（來自 *h₂ey-（意為「年齡；生命」））+ *h₁én（意為「在」）。

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or at the age of adolescence; at the stage between being a child and an adult.

examples.text: We have three adolescent children.
examples.translation: 我們有三個青少年子女。

examples.text: The majority of adolescent drug users are bored.
examples.translation: 大多數青少年吸毒者感到無聊。

examples.text: The adolescent giraffe was banished from the herd.

examples.text: Adolescent boys and girls.

examples.text: This transitional phase, marked by profound adolescent changes, demands significant emotional resilience from all.
examples.license: AI 產生（標記為 AI 翻譯）

etymology.text: First attested ?1440, from Middle English adolescent, from Middle French adolescent or directly from Latin adolescentem, accusative form of adolescens, present participle of adolēscere (“to become adult, grow up”), from ad- (“to”) + alēscere (“to grow or become nourished”). The adjective first appeared in 1785.
etymology.native: 此詞最早見於 1440 年，源自中古英語 adolescent，來自中古法語 adolescent 或直譯自拉丁語 adolescens（adolescentem 的屬格），意為「成長」，由前綴 ad-（表示「向」）與 alēscere（表示「生長或受養」）組成。形容詞形式始見於 1785 年。

senses.definition: Of, or relating to old age.
Exhibiting the deterioration in mind and body often accompanying old age; doddering.

examples.text: Are you saying I'm senile?
examples.translation: 你說我失智了嗎？

examples.text: I think Tom is senile.
examples.translation: 我認為湯姆失智了。

examples.text: He's gone senile.

examples.text: We'll be old and senile before that happens.

examples.text: My grandpa has become really senile these days.
examples.translation: 我爺爺最近變得非常失智。

examples.text: He had grown senile recently.

etymology.text: 1660s; borrowed from French sénile, from Middle French senile, from Old French senile, from Latin senīlis (“of or pertaining to old age”), from senex (“old man”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”).
etymology.native: 1660 年代，借自法語 sénile，源自中古法語 senile，再源自舊法語 senile，來自拉丁語 senīlis（指老年），源於 senex（老人），最終來自原始印歐語 *sénos（老）。

senses.definition: Reluctant to give details about something sensitive; notably prudish.
Pretending shyness or modesty, especially in an insincere or flirtatious way.
Soft, gentle, hesitating.
Bashful, shy, retiring.
Quiet, reserved, modest.

senses.definition: Not clearly expressed; stated in indefinite terms.
Not having a precise meaning.
Not clearly defined, grasped, or understood; indistinct; slight.
Not clearly felt or sensed; somewhat subconscious.
Not thinking or expressing one’s thoughts clearly or precisely.
Lacking expression; vacant.
Not sharply outlined; hazy.
Wandering; vagrant; vagabond.

senses.definition: Arousing or likely to arouse controversy.
Engaging in or given to controversy; disputatious, argumentative.

senses.definition: Tending to inflame or provoke somebody.
Relating to, causing, or caused by inflammation.

examples.text: His inflammatory comments caught everyone off guard.
examples.translation: 他煽動性的言論讓大家措手不及。

examples.text: Stop being so inflammatory.

examples.text: Inflammatory bowel diseases, such as Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, are extremely painful and can lead to colorectal cancer.
examples.translation: 克隆氏症和潰瘍性結腸炎等發炎性腸道疾病極為疼痛，並可能導致大腸直腸癌。

examples.text: We don't allow inflammatory or provocative content in this forum.
examples.translation: 我們不允許這個論壇出現煽動性或挑釁性的內容。

etymology.native: 由「使發炎、煽動」加形容詞字尾組成。

senses.definition: Causing harm in a stealthy, often gradual, manner.
Intending to entrap; alluring but harmful.
Treacherous.

examples.text: Tom isn't insidious.
examples.translation: 湯姆並非陰險。

examples.text: Tom was insidious.
examples.translation: 湯姆是陰險的。

examples.text: It's a dangerous and insidious animal.
examples.translation: 這是一隻危險且陰險的動物。

examples.text: This is a rare and insidious disease.
examples.translation: 這是一種稀有且陰險的疾病。

examples.text: We are working against an enemy who is very insidious in his methods.
examples.translation: 我們正對抗一位手段極其陰險的敵人。

examples.text: That's a very insidious disease. You don't notice it until it's too late.
examples.translation: 這是一種非常陰險的疾病，你直到太晚才發現。

etymology.text: From Middle French insidieux, from Latin īnsidiōsus (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from īnsidiae (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + -ōsus, from īnsideō (“to sit in or on”), from in (“in, on”) + sedeō (“to sit”).
etymology.native: 源自中世紀法語 insidieux，來自拉丁語 īnsidiōsus（意為「狡猾、巧妙、詭計」），由 īnsidiae（意為「伏擊、計謀」）+ -ōsus 組成，而 īnsideō 意為「坐於或伏於」，源自 in（意為「在、於」）+ sedeō（意為「坐」）。

senses.definition: Exhibiting treachery.
Deceitful; inclined to betray.
Unreliable; dangerous.

examples.text: The way is very treacherous.
examples.translation: 這條路挺險惡。

examples.text: Drive carefully! The roads are treacherous.
examples.translation: 小心駕駛！道路很危險。

examples.text: Heavy snowfall made the roads treacherous.
examples.translation: 大雪使得道路變得危險。

examples.text: The Sahara can be a treacherous desert.
examples.translation: 撒哈拉沙漠可能非常危險。

examples.text: Wet logs make for treacherous footing.
examples.translation: 濕木頭走路容易打滑。

examples.text: The mountains were treacherous and steep.
examples.translation: 那些山嶺險峻且陡峭。

etymology.text: From Old French trecheros, tricheros (“deceitful”), equivalent to treacher + -ous. See treacher.
etymology.native: 源自古法語 trecheros 或 tricheros，意為「欺詐的」，等同於 treacher 加上 -ous。參見 treacher。

senses.definition: Causing horror; terrible; shocking.
Tremendously bad.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.translation: 昨天的天氣壞透了。

examples.text: I have a horrible headache.

senses.definition: Something hung up or spread out to hide or protect the face, or hide an object from view; usually of gauze, crepe, or similar diaphanous material.

A cover; disguise; a mask; a pretense.
The calyptra of mosses.
velum (A circular membrane round the cap of a medusa).
A thin layer of tissue which is attached to or covers a mushroom.
A membrane connecting the margin of the pileus of a mushroom with the stalk; a velum.
An obscuration of the clearness of the tones in pronunciation.
That which separates the living and the spirit world.

examples.text: I'll be wearing a veil.
examples.translation: 我將戴著頭紗。

etymology.text: From Middle English veil, veyl, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French veil (“sail, veil, shroud”) (Francien Old French voil, French voile), Latin vēlum (“cloth, covering”). Displaced Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyre (“veil”) (compare German Schleier). Doublet of velum and voile.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語 veil、veyl，來自盎格魯-諾曼語與古法語 veil（意為「帆、面紗、裹紗」），亦源自拉丁語 vēlum（意為「布、覆蓋物」）。取代了中古英語 scleire、scleyre、sleyre、slyre（意為「面紗」），與德語 Schleier 相關。為 velum 與 voile 的同源詞。

Displaced Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyre (“veil”) (compare German Schleier). Doublet of velum and voile.

senses.definition: The act or state of deliberately not paying attention or caring about something.

Cognate with Saterland Frisian Lak (“lack”), Middle Low German lack, lak (“lack”), Dutch lak (“lack, deficiency, calumny”), Icelandic lakur (“lacking”). Related also to Middle Dutch laken (“to
etymology.native: 源自中古英語（lack、lakke、lak），來自古英語（*læc）「缺乏」，再上溯至原始日耳曼語（*laką、*lakaz）「鬆弛」，與（*lakkōną）「責備」有關。與荷蘭語（lak）「缺乏、誹謗」、冰島語（lakur）「缺乏的」同源。

senses.definition: The state of being indifferent.

Unemotional apathy.
A lack of enthusiasm.

examples.translation: 他很有求知慾。

examples.text: Knowledge is not heritable.
examples.translation: 知識不是遺傳的。

examples.text: She has an encyclopedic knowledge of cooking.
examples.translation: 她是一部活生生的廚藝百科全書。

examples.text: Some consider language as a form of knowledge.
examples.translation: 有些人認為語言是一種知識的形式。

examples.text: Mary made a cake without her mother's knowledge.
examples.translation: 瑪莉不讓母親知道，自己做了一個蛋糕。

examples.text: He has a good reading knowledge of French.
examples.translation: 他能很好地讀懂法語。

etymology.text: From Middle English knowleche, knaweleche, cnawlece (“knowledge”), from knowen (“to know, recognise”) + -leche. Related to Middle English knowlechen (“to find out, acknowledge”). For more on the Middle English suffix -leche, compare freelage. Compare also Old English cnāwelǣċ, cnāwelǣċing (“acknowledging, acknowledgement”).
etymology.native: 源自中古英語（knowleche、knaweleche）「知識」，由（knowen）「知道、認出」加（-leche）組成。與中古英語（knowlechen）「發現、承認」有關。比較古英語（cnāwelǣċ）「承認」。

senses.definition: The power, right, or authority to interpret and apply the law.
The power or right to exercise authority.
The power or right to perform some action as part of applying the law.
The authority of a sovereign power to govern or legislate.
The limits or territory within which authority may be exercised.

examples.text: This case is outside my jurisdiction.
Their jurisdiction covers Algiers.
It's outside your jurisdiction.
Our jurisdiction doesn't reach there.
The judge said that the case was outside of his jurisdiction.
He shopped around for a jurisdiction in which his suit was almost guaranteed to win.

relations.native: （表示過去該做卻沒做的事）本來可以

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin iūrisdictiō.

senses.definition: Land that is suitable for farming and agricultural production.

examples.text: Ohio is all forests and farmland.
examples.translation: 俄亥俄州全境皆為森林與農田。

examples.text: Algeria's farmland is wonderful.
examples.translation: 阿爾及利亞的農田非常優美。

examples.text: Here where these houses are used to be farmland.
examples.translation: 這裡原先這些房屋所在之地，都是農田。

examples.text: The wood was cleared to make farmland.
examples.translation: 林木被清除，以便開墾成農田。

examples.text: The basin of a river usually has rich farmland.
examples.translation: 河流的河谷通常擁有豐沃的農田。

examples.text: Tom stood on the edge of his farmland.
examples.translation: 湯姆站在他農田的邊緣。

etymology.text: From farm + land.
etymology.native: 來自 farm 與 land 的組合。

senses.definition: The quality of being available.
That which is available.

examples.text: Mennad's availability has changed.
Mennad's availability changed.
What’s your availability?
Contact us to check availability.
I will plan my business trip according to Tom's availability.
Availability may vary by region and device compatibility.
examples.translation: 實際提供內容可能因地區與裝置相容性而異。

etymology.text: From available + -ity; attested since the early 1800s.

senses.definition: A heroic or extraordinary deed.
An achievement.
A program or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability in other software.
An action or technique that takes advantage of the conditions of a video game to gain an advantage, or to disadvantage others.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: Her rescue of the drowning child was a heroic exploit, remembered for generations.
examples.license: AI 產生（標記為 AI 翻譯）

examples.text: The astronaut’s spacewalk was an exploit of courage, defying gravity and fear.
examples.license: AI 產生（標記為 AI 翻譯）

examples.text: The first trek to the summit of Mount Everest was a stunning exploit.
examples.translation: 首次登頂珠穆朗瑪峰的遠征是一場驚人成就。

etymology.text: From Old French esploit (noun), esploitier (verb).
etymology.native: 源自古法語 esploit（名詞），esploitier（動詞）

senses.definition: To use (something) to someone's advantage, such as one's own benefit or a society's benefit.
To make unfair use of someone else's labor, person, or property to one's own advantage.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: Players using exploits are getting banned.
examples.translation: 使用漏洞的玩家將被封號。

examples.text: Michael exploited people's secrets and weaknesses.
examples.translation: 麥克利用了人們的隱私與弱點。

examples.text: Algeria is exploiting its hydrocarbons.
examples.translation: 阿爾及利亞正開發其石油與天然氣資源。

examples.text: Employers don't create work; they exploit it.
examples.translation: 僱主並非創造工作，而是利用工作。

examples.text: Trust is violated when adults exploit minors.
examples.translation: 當大人利用未成年人時，信任便被破壞。

examples.text: If you exploit workers, you will be castrated.
examples.translation: 若你剝削工人，你將被剝奪生殖能力。

etymology.text: From Old French esploit (noun), esploitier (verb).
etymology.native: 源自古法語 esploit（名詞），esploitier（動詞）

senses.definition: A relatively rare or difficult accomplishment.

examples.text: The player performed a wonderful feat.
examples.translation: 那名球員展現了精彩的技藝。

examples.text: Felix was boating about his feats.
examples.translation: 費利克斯在遊船上展示他的技藝。

examples.text: He imagines he's achieved a feat!
examples.translation: 他想像自己已達成一項偉業！

examples.text: Her skating performance was a regular feat.
examples.translation: 她的滑冰表現是一項常規的技藝。

examples.text: I don't know how he managed such a feat.
examples.translation: 我不知道他是如何完成這項偉業的。

examples.text: You've got to give him credit; that's no easy feat.
examples.translation: 你得給他點讚；這可不是件容易的事。

etymology.text: From Middle English [Term?], from Anglo-Norman fet (“action, deed”), from Old French fait, from Latin factum, from facere (“to do, to make”). Doublet of fact.
etymology.native: 源於中古英語，來自安格洛 - 諾曼語的「動作、行為」，再源自古法語 fait，拉丁語 factum，意為「做、製造」。與 fact 同源。

senses.definition: To remove (rock or ore) from the ground.
To dig into, for ore or metal.
To sow mines (the explosive devices) in (an area).
To damage (a vehicle or ship) with a mine (an explosive device).
To dig a tunnel or hole; to burrow in the earth.
To dig away, or otherwise remove, the substratum or foundation of; to lay a mine under; to sap; to undermine.
To ruin or destroy by slow degrees or secret means.
To tap into.
To earn new units of cryptocurrency by doing certain calculations.
To pick one's nose.

examples.text: They mined iron in this town for 350 years.
Tom's hands are stronger than mine.
examples.translation: 湯姆的雙手比我的強壯。

examples.text: Can I borrow a pen? Mine's on its last legs.
examples.translation: 能借枝筆嗎？我這枝要不行了。

examples.text: Tim's motorbike is far more expensive than mine is.
examples.translation: 提姆的機車比我的貴多了。

examples.text: "Don't worry," Dima attempted to put the woman at ease. "It's not mine."
examples.translation: 「別擔心，」狄馬嘗試讓店員鎮定下來：「那不是我的血。」

etymology.text: From Middle English min, myn, from Old English mīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mīn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *méynos.

senses.definition: A public gathering or mass meeting that is not mainly a protest and is organized to inspire enthusiasm for a cause.
An event in which competitors drive through a series of timed special stages at intervals. The winner is the driver who completes all stages with the shortest cumulative time.
A protest or demonstration for or against something, but often with speeches and often without marching, especially in North America.
senses.native: 抗議或示威活動，通常包含演說，但不一定伴隨遊行，尤其在北美地區

senses.definition: A sequence of strokes between serving and scoring a point.
senses.native: 發球與得分之間的一系列擊球動作

senses.definition: A recovery after a decline in prices (said of the market, stocks, etc.)
senses.native: 價格下跌後的回升（適用於市場、股票等）

senses.definition: Good-humoured raillery.

examples.text: They're organizing rallies everywhere.
examples.translation: 他們到處都在組織集會。

examples.text: His party's rally was in September.
examples.translation: 他的黨派集會在九月舉行。

examples.text: There were at most twenty people at the rally.
examples.translation: 集會上最多只有二十人。

examples.text: Bouteflika banned political rallies in Algiers.
examples.translation: 布特弗利卡禁止在阿爾及爾舉行政治集會。

examples.text: Do you really want to go to the pep rally?
examples.translation: 你真的要去參加熱情集會嗎？

examples.text: You can attend school assemblies and pep rallies.
examples.translation: 你可以參加學校集會和熱情集會。

etymology.text: From Middle French rallier (French rallier), from Old French ralier, from Latin prefix re- + ad + ligare (“to bind; to ally”).
etymology.native: 源於中古法語 rallier，後來自舊法語 ralier，由拉丁語前綴 re- 加上 ligare（綁縛；結盟）組成。

senses.definition: The act of utilizing something; industry.
The improper use of something for selfish purposes.
The act or result of forcibly depriving someone of something to which they have a right.
senses.native: 強行剝奪他人合法權益的行為或結果

senses.definition: The marketing and promotion of a film.
A genre of media focused on lurid depictions of topical social issues such as violence, sexuality and marginalized groups.
senses.native: 聚焦於暴力、性與邊緣群體等社會議題露骨描繪的媒體類型

examples.text: This exploitation needs to stop.
examples.translation: 這種剝削必須停止。

examples.text: I fought against the exploitation of Brazil.
examples.translation: 我反對對巴西的剝削。

examples.text: Islam hates the exploitation of the poor.
examples.translation: 伊斯蘭教憎恨對貧窮者的剝削。

examples.text: Privacy protects the individual from exploitation.
examples.translation: 隱私保護個人免受剝削。

examples.text: The oppression of women is closely linked to capitalist exploitation.
examples.translation: 女性受壓迫與資本主義剝削密切相關。

examples.text: In this country we condemn child exploitation.
examples.translation: 我國譴責兒童剝削。

etymology.text: Borrowed from French exploitation, from exploiter (“exploit”), from Latin explicō (“unfold, deploy”). By surface analysis, exploit + -ation.
etymology.native: 源自法語 exploitation，意為「利用」，再追溯至拉丁語 explicō（展開、部署）。依字面分析可視為 exploit 加上 -ation。

senses.definition: Conditions suitable for an organism or population of organisms to live.
A range; a place where a species naturally occurs.
A terrestrial or aquatic area distinguished by geographic, abiotic and biotic features, whether entirely natural or semi-natural.
A place in which a person lives.

examples.text: Trees are habitats for animals.
He observed pandas in their natural habitat.
Here, heathers are in their natural habitat.
A giraffe's coat is adapted to its habitat.
I would like to see a giraffe in its habitat.
The habitat of seals is typically coastal areas.

etymology.text: From Latin habitat (“it dwells, lives”), the 3rd person singular present active indicative form of habitō (“to live or dwell”). In Linnaeus and similar authors, the geographical ranges of species were customarily denoted in Latin by a sentence beginning with "Habitat", e.g. "Habitat in Europa" ("It lives in Europe"), and it thus became the convention to refer to the geographical range as the "habitat". Compare the English derivations of exit, floruit, ignoramus, and tenet from Latin finite verbs

senses.definition: Any binary compound of chlorine and another element or radical.
Any salt of hydrochloric acid.
The anionic form of a chlorine atom.

examples.text: Silver chloride is not completely water-soluble.
In culinary, can you substitute sodium bromide for sodium chloride?
Sodium chloride is commonly known as salt.
Table salt, primarily composed of sodium chloride, can be used both to season and to preserve food.

etymology.text: From chlor(ine) + -ide, coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1812.

senses.definition: The divide between land and a body of water.
The line on a map that illustrates this.

examples.text: A lone island could be seen from the shoreline.
examples.translation: 一座孤島從海岸線上可見。

examples.text: Tom continued walking along the shoreline.
examples.translation: 湯姆沿著海岸線繼續行走。

examples.text: Tom and Mary walked along the shoreline.
examples.translation: 湯姆和瑪麗沿著海岸線散步。

examples.text: This is a really lonely stretch of shoreline.
examples.translation: 這是一處非常孤獨的海岸線地段。

examples.text: The shoreline and coastal wetlands provide critical feeding and resting habitat for shorebirds and waders.
examples.translation: 海岸線與沿海濕地為岸鳥和涉禽提供了關鍵的覓食與棲息地。

examples.text: The fierce pounding of the waves during the storm washed tonnes of shoreline into the ocean.
examples.translation: 風暴期間海浪猛烈拍打，將數噸岸邊泥土沖入海洋。

etymology.text: From shore + line.
etymology.native: 「岸」加上「線」組成。

senses.definition: A carved object.
The act or craft of producing a carved object.

examples.text: Atuqtuaq is excellent at soapstone carving.
examples.translation: 阿圖克塔克擅長石雕。

examples.text: That's really a good carving.
examples.translation: 這件雕刻真的很好。

examples.text: Tom likes carving pipes.
examples.translation: 湯姆喜歡雕刻煙管。

examples.text: Tom pulled out his knife and started carving.
examples.translation: 湯姆拔出刀子開始雕刻。

examples.text: Tom participated in the ice carving competition.
examples.translation: 湯姆參加了冰雕比賽。

examples.text: The river knows no bounds, carving its own path.
examples.translation: 河流無邊無際，自行開闢道路。

senses.definition: To fatigue, tire, or weary (someone or something).
To treat (someone or something) like a jade; to spurn.
senses.native: 像對待駑馬一樣對待（某人或某物）；拒絕

senses.definition: To make (someone or something) contemptible and ridiculous.
senses.native: 使（某人或某事）顯得可鄙、可笑

examples.text: You just feel jaded!
Don't tell me you're only 18 and already jaded?
You're jaded, not depressed.
You sound somewhat jaded.
It's easy to feel jaded if you don't see the variety in life and of this world.
Tom is jaded and cynical.

etymology.text: Borrowed from French le jade, rebracketing of earlier l'éjade (“jade”), from Spanish piedra de ijada (“flank stone”), via Vulgar Latin *iliata from Latin ilia (“flank”). (Jade was thought to cure pains in the side.)
etymology.native: 借自法語「玉」，由較早的形式重新切分而來，源自西班牙語「側腹之石」，經通俗拉丁語來自拉丁語「側腹」（古人認為玉能治側腹疼痛）。

senses.definition: An upright open container used mainly for displaying fresh, dried, or artificial flowers.
The body of the Corinthian capital.
senses.native: （建築）柱身，科林斯柱頭的主體

senses.definition: an exon of NCAM; it is thought to correlate with an inhibition of the neurite outgrowth-promoting properties of this protein
senses.native: （生化）外顯子，神經細胞黏附分子的一段，與抑制神經突生長有關

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: This broken vase cannot be repaired.
examples.translation: 這個壞掉的花瓶無法修復了。

examples.text: The vase was broken to pieces.
examples.translation: 花瓶被摔成了碎片。

examples.text: Put some water into the vase.
examples.translation: 在花瓶裡裝些水。

examples.text: Hold the vase in both hands.
examples.translation: 用雙手握著花瓶。

examples.text: I must apologize to you for breaking the vase.
examples.translation: 我把你的花瓶打破了，真對不起。

examples.text: There are some beautiful roses in the vase.
examples.translation: 有一些漂亮的花在花瓶。

etymology.text: Borrowed from Middle French vase, from Latin vās. Doublet of vas.
etymology.native: 借自中古法語，來自拉丁語「容器」。與「管（解剖）」為同源異形詞。

senses.definition: To protect, to defend.
To shelter; to protect oneself.
To protect from the influence of.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: Tom shielded his eyes from the bright light.
examples.translation: 湯姆用雙手遮住眼睛免受強光刺激。

examples.text: Tom and Mary shielded their eyes from the sun.
examples.translation: 湯姆與瑪麗都遮住眼睛避開陽光。

examples.text: She shielded the ball from the opponent.
examples.translation: 她將球從對手手中擋下。

examples.text: His black sunglasses shielded his eyes from the sun's glare.
examples.translation: 他戴著黑框太陽眼鏡，遮擋陽光刺眼。

examples.text: Sunscreen shields against the harmful effects of solar rays.
examples.translation: 太陽防曬霜能抵禦太陽輻射的傷害。

etymology.text: From Middle English scheld, shelde, from Old English scield (“shield”), from Proto-West Germanic *skeldu, from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“cut, split”).
etymology.native: 源自中世紀英文 scheld、shelde，來自古英文 scield（意為「盾牌」），源自原始西日耳曼語 *skeldu，再源自原始德語 *skelduz（意為「盾牌」），最終源自原始印歐語 *(s)kelH-（意為「切開、分裂」）。

senses.definition: A butt or mark to shoot at, as for practice, or to test the accuracy of a firearm, or the force of a projectile.
A goal or objective.
The codomain of a function; the object at which a morphism points.
The translated version of a document, or the language into which translation occurs.
A person (or group of people) that a person or organization is trying to employ or to have as a customer, audience etc.
A system or platform for which software is developed.
An object of criticism or ridicule.
A person, place, or thing that is frequently attacked, criticized, or ridiculed.
A kind of small shield or buckler, used as a defensive weapon in war.
A shield resembling the Roman scutum, larger than the modern buckler.
A bearing representing a buckler.
The pattern or arrangement of a series of hits made by a marksman on a butt or mark.
The sliding crosspiece, or vane, on a leveling staff.
A conspicuous disk attached to a switch lever to show its position, or for use as a signal.
the number of runs that the side batting last needs to score in the final innings in order to win
The tenor of a metaphor.
A thin cut; a slice; specifically, of lamb, a piece consisting of the neck and breast joints.
A tassel or pendant.
A shred; a tatter.

examples.text: Target was targeted by cybercriminals.
examples.translation: （Target）百貨成了網路罪犯的目標。

examples.text: The first attack missed the target.
examples.translation: 第一次攻擊錯過了目標。

examples.text: No matter how low the target, always aim higher.
examples.translation: 無事掘小，小事掘大。

examples.text: Appreciate the little things in life - they will bring you to a bigger end target.
examples.translation: 欣賞生活中的小事，它們的總合很是宏大。

examples.text: Lions often target sick or injured animals.
examples.translation: 獅子常以生病或受傷的動物為目標。

examples.text: He picked up the rifle and aimed it at the target.
examples.translation: 他拿起步槍，瞄準目標。

etymology.text: From Middle French targette, targuete, diminutive of targe (“light shield”), from Old French, from Frankish *targa (“buckler”), akin to Old Norse targa (“small round shield”) (whence also Old English targe, targa (“shield”)) from Proto-Germanic *targǭ (“edge”), from Proto-Indo-European *derǵʰ- (“fenced lot”). Akin to Old High German zarga (“side wall, rim”) (German Zarge (“frame”)), Spanish tarjeta (“card”).
etymology.native: 源自中古法語（targette、targuete），是（targe）「輕盾」的指小形式，來自古法語，再源自法蘭克語（*targa）「圓盾」，與古諾斯語（targa）「小圓盾」同源，最終可溯至原始日耳曼語（*targǭ）「邊緣」。與古高地德語（zarga）「側壁、邊緣」、西班牙語（tarjeta）「卡片」同源。

senses.definition: A disguise or covering up.
A pattern on clothing consisting of irregularly shaped patches that are either greenish/brownish, brownish/whitish, or bluish/whitish, as used by ground combat forces.
The resemblance of an organism to its surroundings for avoiding detection.
Clothes made from camouflage fabric, for concealment in combat or hunting.
The act of disguising.
The use of natural or artificial material on personnel, objects, or tactical positions with the aim of confusing, misleading, or evading the enemy.
senses.native: （軍事）偽裝，用天然或人造材料掩蔽人員、物資或陣地，以迷惑或躲避敵人

examples.text: Tom usually wears a camouflage jacket.
examples.translation: 湯姆通常穿著一件迷彩夾克。

examples.text: Martino was wearing a camouflage baseball cap.
examples.translation: 馬丁諾戴著一頂迷彩棒球帽。

examples.text: Most of the soldiers wore camouflage uniforms.
examples.translation: 大多數士兵穿著迷彩服。

examples.text: My racial composition is just a camouflage.
examples.translation: 我的種族組成不過是一層掩飾。

examples.text: The waitress didn't see Tom because he was wearing a camouflage shirt.
examples.translation: 女服務生沒看到湯姆，因為他穿著一件迷彩襯衫。

examples.text: The hunter wore camouflage clothing.
examples.translation: 獵人穿著迷彩服裝。

etymology.text: Unadapted borrowing from French camouflage, from camoufler (“to veil, disguise”), alteration (due to camouflet (“smoke blown in one's face”)) of Italian camuffare (“to muffle the head”), from ca- (from Italian capo (“head”)) + muffare (“to muffle”), from Medieval Latin muffula, muffla (“muff”). This Medieval Latin, from which there is also English muffle, is either derived from a Frankish *molfell (“soft garment made of hide”) from *mol (“softened, forworn”) (akin to Old High German molawēn (“to
etymology.native: 「迷彩」一詞源自法語 camoufler，該詞又由義大利語 camuffare 改寫而成。

senses.definition: Disparaging.
Tending to derogate
Reducing the power or value of (a governmental body, etc); detracting from.
Being or pertaining to a derogatory clause.
Lessening the worth of (a person, etc); expressing derogation; insulting.

examples.text: Tom made some derogatory remarks.
examples.translation: 湯姆說了一些侮辱性的話。

examples.text: Tom said nothing derogatory.
examples.translation: 湯姆沒說任何侮辱性的話。

examples.text: They never said anything derogatory about Islam.
examples.translation: 他們從未對伊斯蘭說過任何侮辱性話。

examples.text: Fat is a derogatory term.
examples.translation: 胖是個侮辱性的詞。

examples.text: Rodrigo's social media profiles were flooded with offensive and derogatory comments.

examples.text: This event benefits no one.
examples.translation: 這件事對誰都沒有好處。

examples.text: We postponed the event.
examples.translation: 我們把活動延期了。

examples.text: This event has ended.
examples.translation: 這場活動結束了。

examples.text: The event is still fresh in our memory.
examples.translation: 那件事在我們的腦海中還記憶猶新。

etymology.text: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”), short form of ex + veniō (“come”); related to venture, advent, convent, invent, convene, evene, etc.
etymology.native: 來自中世紀法語 event，源自拉丁語 ēventus（「事件、發生」），自 ēveniō（「發生、出現、出現」），源自 ē（「從、出自」），是 ex + veniō（「來」）的縮寫；與 venture、advent、convent、invent、convene、evene 等詞相關。

senses.definition: That which is produced or occurs as a result of an event or process.
The result of a random trial. An element of a sample space.
The anticipated or desired results or evidence of a learning experience.
The scoreline; the result.

examples.text: Are intentions more important than outcomes?
The outcome didn't meet our expectations.
Could they have prevented this outcome?
What options do I have to change the outcome?
The game's outcome hangs on his performance.
Any way you do, the outcome is no different.

etymology.text: From out + come.

senses.definition: Something which is related to, or in some way affects, a fact or event.
An event; a fact; a particular incident, occurrence, or condition (status).
Condition in regard to worldly estate; state of property; situation; surroundings.
Evasive or indirect language; circumlocution.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: Mary grew up in straitened circumstances.
The family's circumstances are not easy.
She always adapted to new circumstances.
Under such circumstances, we cannot succeed.
examples.translation: 在這種情況下，我們沒辦法成功。

examples.text: Under no circumstances must you leave the room.
examples.translation: 在任何情況下你都不能離開這個房間。

examples.text: The circumstances did not allow me to go abroad.
examples.translation: 情況不允許我出國。

etymology.text: From Middle English circumstaunce, from Old French circonstance, from Latin circumstantia.

senses.definition: A thing or being, event or process, perceptible through senses; or a fact or occurrence thereof.
A knowable thing or event (e.g. by inference, especially in science).
A kind or type of phenomenon (sense 1 or 2).
Appearance; a perceptible aspect of something that is mutable.
A fact or event considered very unusual, curious, or astonishing by those who witness it.
A wonderful or very remarkable person or thing.
An experienced object whose constitution reflects the order and conceptual structure imposed upon it by the human mind (especially by the powers of perception and understanding).

pronunciations.attribution: No machine-readable source provided. Own work assumed (based on copyright claims).

examples.text: Time dilation is an interesting phenomenon.
Michael Jordan was a phenomenon.
This phenomenon is nothing new.
It's a phenomenon I've never seen before.
examples.translation: 這是我以前從未見過的現象。

examples.text: Many of Europe's metropolises are plagued by the donut phenomenon.
examples.translation: 許多歐洲的大都市飽受「甜甜圈現象」困擾。

examples.text: An eclipse of the moon is a rare phenomenon.
examples.translation: 月食是一種罕見的現象。

etymology.text: From Late Latin phaenomenon (“appearance”), from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”), neuter present middle participle of φαίνω (phaínō, “I show”).

senses.definition: An answer or reply, or something in the nature of an answer or reply.
The act of responding or replying; reply: as, to speak in response to a question.
An oracular answer.
A verse, sentence, phrase, or word said or sung by the choir or congregation in sequence or reply to the priest or officiant.
A versicle or anthem said or sung during or after a lection; a respond or responsory.
A reply to an objection in formal disputation.
An online advertising performance metric representing one click-through from an online ad to its destination URL.
A reaction to a stimulus or provocation.

examples.text: When pushed for an answer, she gave the stock response.
examples.translation: 被追問時，她給了一個制式回答。

examples.text: His responses have slowed with age.
I'm sorry for the late response.
examples.translation: 我很抱歉回覆晚了。

examples.text: What's Algeria's response to the coronavirus?
examples.translation: 阿爾及利亞對新冠病毒的應對是什麼？

examples.text: Our proposals met with little response.
examples.translation: 我們的提案幾乎沒有得到回應。

examples.text: She made no response to my question.
examples.translation: 她沒有回答我的問題。

etymology.text: From Middle English respounse, respons, from Old French respons, respuns, responce, ultimately from the Latin respōnsum, a nominal use of the neuter form of respōnsus, the perfect passive participle of respondeō, from re (“again”) + spondeō (“promise”). Doublet of responsum.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語（respounse、respons），來自古法語（respons、responce），最終源自拉丁語（respōnsum），是（respondeō）的完成式被動分詞（respōnsus）中性形式的名詞用法，由（re）「再」加（spondeō）「承諾」組成。與（responsum）為雙式詞。

senses.definition: A beginning; a first move.
A new development; a fresh approach to something; a new way of dealing with a problem.
The ability to act first or on one's own.
An issue to be voted on, brought to the ballot by a sufficient number of signatures from among the voting public.

examples.text: Companies welcome workers who take initiative.
Take initiative in starting conversations.
The initiative is punishable.
Boldi even praised Martha for her initiative.
There are very many initiatives and projects.
He usually takes the initiative in discussions.

etymology.text: From French initiative, from Medieval Latin *initiativus (“serving to initiate”), from Late Latin initiare (“to begin, to initiate”), from Latin initium (“beginning”), from ineo (“enter, begin”). By surface analysis, initiate + -ive.

senses.definition: The quality of being contingent, of happening by chance.
A possibility; something which may or may not happen. A chance occurrence, especially in finance, unexpected expenses.

An amount of money which a party to a contract has to pay to the other party (usually the supplier of a major project to the client) if they do not fulfill the contract according to the specification.
A statement which is neither a tautology nor a contradiction.

examples.text: We should have a contingency plan.
Does Tom have a contingency plan?
Do you have a contingency plan?
We need to make a contingency plan.
We should be prepared for all contingencies.
We should be prepared for that contingency.

etymology.text: From contingence + -y (16th century).

senses.definition: Having great enthusiasm, passion and energy.
Being in a state of higher energy.
Having an erection; erect.
Sexually aroused.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: I'm too excited to eat anything.
examples.translation: 我興奮得吃不下任何東西。

examples.text: I'm too excited to sleep.
examples.translation: 我激動得睡不著。

etymology.text: From excite + -ed.
etymology.native: 來自 excite + -ed。

senses.definition: In a state of panic, worry, frenzy, or rush.
Extremely energetic.
Insane, mentally unstable.

examples.text: They looked like they were frantic.
examples.translation: 他們看起來很慌亂。

examples.text: Tom was frantic, but Mary wasn't.
examples.translation: 湯姆很慌亂，但瑪麗不是。

examples.translation: 瑪麗看起來很慌亂。

examples.translation: 湯姆告訴我他認為瑪麗很慌亂。

examples.translation: 你看起來不像湯姆那麼慌亂。

examples.text: Tom doesn't seem to be as frantic as Mary seems to be.
examples.translation: 湯姆看起來不像瑪麗那麼慌亂。

etymology.text: From Middle English frantike, frentik, variant of frenetik, from Old French frenetique, from Late Latin phreneticus, alteration of phreniticus, from φρενιτικός (phrenitikós, “mad, suffering from inflammation of the brain”), from φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”), from φρήν (phrḗn, “the brain”). Doublet of frenetic and phrenitic.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語，由舊法語、晚拉丁語及希臘語演化而來，意指腦部發炎或瘋狂。

senses.definition: That reacts or responds to a stimulus.
That readily takes part in reactions.
Characterized by induction or capacitance rather than resistance.
Reacting to the past rather than anticipating the future, not predictive.

examples.text: We'd much rather be proactive than reactive.
Retroactive jealousy is more toxic than reactive jealousy.
Mary's realisation that she was gay plunged her into a reactive depression.
This is an ideal application for argon gas, whose inertness gives it a huge safety advantage over more reactive gases.
Are humans good at reactive aggression?
Sodium is a reactive metal.

etymology.text: From react + -ive.

senses.definition: The state or act of contemning; the feeling or attitude of regarding someone or something as inferior, base, or worthless; scorn, disdain.
The state of being despised or dishonored; disgrace.
Open disrespect or willful disobedience of the authority of a court of law or legislative body.

examples.text: He is below contempt.
examples.translation: 他讓人討厭透頂。

examples.text: Familiarity breeds contempt and children.
examples.translation: 熟悉便生厭惡與孩子氣。

examples.text: Antonio showed nothing but contempt.
examples.translation: 安東尼對此毫不厭惡。

examples.text: I have nothing but contempt for these people.
examples.translation: 我對這些人完全不抱好感，只覺厭惡。

examples.text: I feel nothing but contempt for such behavior.
examples.translation: 對這種行為，我只感到厭惡。

examples.text: Tom's voice expressed the utmost contempt.
examples.translation: 湯姆的語氣充滿了最極端的厭惡。

etymology.text: From Latin contemptus (“scorn”), from contemnō (“to scorn, despise”), from com- + temnō (“to despise”). Displaced native Old English forsewennes.
etymology.native: 此詞源自拉丁語 contemptus（意為「蔑視」），由 contemnō（意為「蔑視、鄙視」）衍生，而 contemnō 由 com- + temnō（意為「鄙視」）構成。原為古英語 forsewennes 的替代詞。

senses.definition: Middlemost; located at the center.
Emotionally stable, calm, serene; having a balanced mind.

examples.text: He's so self-centered and obnoxious.
examples.translation: 他太以自我為中心，而且很討人厭。

examples.text: She's very self-centered, isn't she?
examples.translation: 她非常以自我為中心，不是嗎？

examples.text: Their talks centered on their trip.
examples.translation: 他們的對話圍繞著旅行展開。

examples.text: Self-centered people like to devalue others.
examples.translation: 以自我為中心的人喜歡低估他人。

examples.text: Elias decided he would never be self-centered.
examples.translation: 埃利亞斯決定他再也不要以自我為中心。

examples.text: He centered his business on the metropolitan area.
examples.translation: 他將生意重心放在大都市地區。

senses.definition: simple past and past participle of center

pronunciations.value: S EH1 N T ER0 D

senses.definition: To move things physically towards the centre; to consolidate or concentrate
To move power to a single, central authority
To make something focal, the most important

examples.text: Algeria's government is too centralized.
Algeria had a strong centralized bureaucracy.
Algeria should stop centralized planning.
Effective public policy is not a simple matter of centralize or decentralize, subsidize or privatize, regulate or deregulate.
The Russian government centralized the distribution of food.

etymology.text: From central + -ize.

senses.definition: The quality of being reliable, dependable, or trustworthy.

the ability to measure the same thing consistently (of a measurement indicating the degree to which the measure is consistent); that is, repeated measurements would give the same result (See also validity).
measurable time of work before failure

examples.text: His reliability is often in question.
Can you vouch for Tom's reliability?
All he has going for him is his reliability.
He has a good name for reliability.
Cosby's argument concerns the reliability of the Hette Manuscript.
Your reliability has been questionable lately.

etymology.text: From reliable + -ity.

senses.definition: A phase.
A place where anything is publicly exhibited, or a remarkable affair occurs; the scene.
The succession of rock strata laid down in a single age on the geologic time scale.
An internship.
The notional space within which stereo sounds are positioned, determining where they will appear to come from when played back.
The profession of an actor.
One of the portions of a device (such as a rocket or thermonuclear weapon) which are used or activated in a particular order, one after another.
A platform; a surface, generally elevated, upon which show performances or other public events are given.
A floor or storey of a house.
A floor elevated for the convenience of mechanical work, etc.; scaffolding; staging.
A platform, often floating, serving as a kind of wharf.
A stagecoach, an enclosed horsedrawn carriage used to carry passengers; the service that such coaches provide; a company that operates such service.
A place of rest on a regularly travelled road; a station, way station; a place appointed for a relay of horses.
A degree of advancement in a journey; one of several portions into which a road or course is marked off; the distance between two places of rest on a road.
The number of an electronic circuit’s block, such as a filter, an amplifier, etc.
The place on a microscope where the slide is located for viewing.
A level; one of the areas making up the game.
senses.native: 等級；構成遊戲的某個區域（關卡）

senses.definition: An unpaid internship in a restaurant where a cook or chef is exposed to new culinary techniques.

examples.translation: 有些音樂家會在舞台上喝酒。

examples.text: There are different stages of colonization.
examples.translation: 殖民過程分為不同階段。

examples.text: Are there any famous musicians on the stage?
examples.translation: 舞臺上有著名音樂家嗎？

examples.text: The stage was sprinkled with flower petals.
examples.translation: 舞臺上撒了花瓣。

examples.text: Shakespeare compared the world to a stage.
examples.translation: 莎士比亞把世界比喻成一個舞台。

examples.text: Putin will be a pariah on the international stage.
examples.translation: 普丁將成為國際舞台上的棄兒。

etymology.text: From Middle English stage, from Old French estage (“dwelling, residence; position, situation, condition”), from Old French ester (“to be standing, be located”). Cognate with Old English stæþþan (“to make staid, stay”), Old Norse steðja (“to place, provide, confirm, allow”), Old English stede (“state, status, standing, place, station, site”). More at stead. Doublet of étage.
etymology.native: 「stage」源自中世紀英語，來源為古法語 estage（意為「居所、位置、狀況」），再源自古法語 ester（意為「站立、位於」）。與古英語 stæþþan（意為「使站穩、停留」）、古諾斯語 steðja（意為「放置、提供、確認、允許」）、古英語 stede（意為「狀態、地位、位置、站位」）同源。詳見 stead。此詞亦為 étage 的同源詞。

senses.definition: To produce on a stage, to perform a play.
To arrange in a manner intended to deceive.
senses.native: 以欺騙為目的進行安排（造假、作假）

senses.definition: To furnish and decorate (a property) to make it more appealing to potential buyers.
senses.native: 為（房產）佈置與裝飾，使其更吸引潛在買家（布置）

senses.definition: To orchestrate; to carry out.
To place in position to prepare for use.
senses.native: 將物件置於就緒位置，準備使用

senses.definition: To determine what stage (a disease, etc.) has progressed to
senses.native: 判定（疾病等）發展到哪個階段（分期）

senses.definition: To jettison a spent stage of a multistage rocket or other launch vehicle and light the engine(s) of the stage above it.
senses.native: 拋棄多節火箭或其他運載工具已耗盡的級段，並點燃上一級的引擎（分級）

senses.definition: To work an internship, usually as a chef or waiter.
senses.native: （加拿大、美）擔任實習生，通常為廚師或服務生

senses.definition: To work as an unpaid intern in a restaurant.
senses.native: 在餐廳擔任無薪實習生

examples.text: The actor went on stage to deliver his lines.

etymology.text: From Middle English stage, from Old French estage (“dwelling, residence; position, situation, condition”), from Old French ester (“to be standing, be located”). Cognate with Old English stæþþan (“to make staid, stay”), Old Norse steðja (“to place, provide, confirm, allow”), Old English stede (“state, status, standing, place, station, site”). More at stead. Doublet of étage.
etymology.native: 「stage」源自中世紀英語，來源為古法語 estage（意為「居所、位置、狀況」），再源自古法語 ester（意為「站立、位於」）。與古英語 stæþþan（意為「使站穩、停留」）、古諾斯語 steðja（意為「放置、提供、確認、允許」）、古英語 stede（意為「狀態、地位、位置、站位」）同源。詳見 stead。此詞亦為 étage 的同源詞。

senses.definition: A distinguishable part of a sequence or cycle occurring over time.
That which is exhibited to the eye; the appearance which anything manifests, especially any one among different and varying appearances of the same object.
Any appearance or aspect of an object of mental apprehension or view.

A particular appearance or state in a regularly recurring cycle of changes with respect to quantity of illumination or form, or the absence, of a body's illuminated disk. Illustrated in Wikipedia's article Lunar phase.

Any one point or portion in a recurring series of changes, as in the changes of motion of one of the particles constituting a wave or vibration; one portion of a series of such changes, in distinction from a contrasted portion, as the portion on one side of a position of equilibrium, in contrast with that on the opposite side.

A component in a material system that is distinguished by chemical composition and/or physical state (solid, liquid or gas) and/or crystal structure. It is delineated from an adjoining phase by an abrupt change in one or more of those conditions.
In certain organisms, one of two or more colour variations characteristic of the species, but independent of the ordinary seasonal and sexual differences, and often also of age.
The period of play between consecutive breakdowns.
A haplotype.

The counterclockwise angle from the positive half of the real number line to the vector pointing to a complex number on an Argand diagram of the complex plane, which has the positive real line pointing right and the positive imaginary number line pointing up.
A distortion caused by a difference in the speed of propagation for different frequencies
In a polyphase electrical power system, one of the power-carrying conductors, or the alternating current carried by it.

etymology.text: Borrowed from New Latin phasis, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”), from φᾰ(ν)- (phă(n)-, root of φαίνω (phaínō, “to bring to light; to appear”)) + -σῐς (-sĭs).

senses.definition: To place a crown on the head of.
To effect a lodgment upon, as upon the crest of the glacis, or the summit of the breach.
To lay the ends of the strands of (a knot) over and under each other.
To formally declare (someone) a king, queen, emperor, etc.

senses.definition: To form the topmost or finishing part of; to complete; to consummate; to perfect.
senses.native: 形成最頂端或最後部分；使完成、圓滿

To have its head's surface appear in the vaginal opening during the birthing process.

senses.definition: To widen the opening of the barrel.
To shoot (someone) in the head.
invest with regal power; enthrone
be the culminating event
form the topmost part of
To have its topmost part emerge partially from the body, as a result of heightened internal pressure in the bowels.
To struggle to hold back an imminent, crowning bowel movement.

examples.text: Charlemagne was crowned by the Pope.
examples.translation: 查理曼大帝由教宗加冕。

examples.text: This majestic mountain range in the heart of south Asia is crowned with snowcapped peaks and draped with vast glaciers.
examples.translation: 這座位於南亞中心的雄偉山脈，山峰白雪皚皚，覆蓋著廣闊的冰川。

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English coroune, from Anglo-Norman corone, from Latin corōna (“crown, wreath”), from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē). Doublet of corona, korona, koruna, krona, króna, and krone. Displaced Old English corenbēag (“crown”) and Middle English kinehelm, kynehelm, from Old English cynehelm (“crown”, literally “kinhelm” or “king's helm”).
etymology.native: 此詞源自中世英文 coroune，來源於盎格魯-諾曼語 corone，再源自拉丁文 corōna（意為「冠冕、花環」），而拉丁文則來自古希臘文 κορώνη（korṓnē）。與 corona、korona、koruna、krona、króna、krone 為同源詞。取代了古英語 corenbēag（意為「冠冕」）及中世英文 kinehelm、kynehelm，這些詞源自古英語 cynehelm（意為「王冠」，字面意為「君主之盔」）

senses.definition: The act or state of being or making something complete; conclusion, accomplishment.
The conclusion of an act of conveyancing concerning the sale of a property.
A forward pass that is successfully caught by the intended receiver.
The act of making a metric space complete by adding points.
The space resulting from such an act.
Synonym of autocomplete.
Orgasm.

etymology.text: From Latin antidotum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίδοτον (antídoton, “antidote, remedy”), Clipping of ἀντίδοτον φάρμακον (antídoton phármakon, “drug given against”), from ἀντιδίδωμι (antidídōmi, “to give in return, repay”), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). senses.definition: A period of one hundred consecutive years; often specifically a numbered period with conventional start and end dates, e.g., the twentieth century, which stretches from (strictly) 1901 through 2000, or (informally) 1900 through 1999. The first century AD was from 1 to 100.

A unit in ancient Roman army, originally of one hundred army soldiers as part of a cohort, later of more varied sizes (but typically containing sixty to seventy or eighty) soldiers or other men (guards, police, firemen), commanded by a centurion.
senses.native: （古羅馬）百人隊，原指一百名士兵的單位，後來人數不定，通常為六十至七十人

senses.definition: A political division of ancient Rome, meeting in the Centuriate Assembly.
senses.native: （古羅馬）百人團，百人團大會中的投票單位

senses.definition: A hundred things of the same kind; a hundred.
A hundred runs scored either by a single player in one innings, or by two players in a partnership.
senses.native: （板球）百分，單人或雙人合作在一局中跑出一百分

senses.definition: A score of one hundred points.
A race a hundred units (as meters, kilometres, miles) in length.
senses.native: 一百單位長度（如公尺、公里、英里）的賽跑

senses.definition: A banknote in the denomination of one hundred dollars.

examples.text: One hundred years is called a century.
examples.translation: 一百年叫做一個世紀。

senses.definition: Rubble, wreckage, scattered remains of something destroyed.
Litter and discarded refuse.
Large rock fragments left by a melting glacier etc.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.translation: 一團塵土與瓦礫騰空而起，在空中盤旋了數分鐘。

etymology.text: Borrowed from French débris, itself from dé- (“de-”) + bris (“broken, crumbled”), or from Middle French debriser (“to break apart”), from Old French debrisier, itself from de- + brisier (“to break apart, shatter, bust”), from Frankish *bristijan, *bristan, *brestan (“to break violently, shatter, bust”), from Proto-Germanic *brestaną (“to break, burst”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrest- (“to separate, burst”). Cognate with Old High German bristan (“to break asunder, burst”), Old English berstan
etymology.native: 此詞源自法語 débris，本身由 dé-（de-）與 bris（破碎、碎裂）組成，或源自中世紀法語 debriser（意為「破碎」），再溯自古法語 debrisier，亦由 de- 與 brisier（意為「破碎、粉碎」）構成，而 brisier 又源自古弗蘭克語 *bristijan、*bristan、*brestan（意為「猛烈破碎、粉碎」），再上溯至古日耳曼語 *brestaną（意為「破碎、爆裂」），最終源自印歐語系 *bʰrest-（意為「分離、爆裂」）。與古高地德語 bristan（意為「撕裂、爆裂」）及古英語 berstan 同源。

senses.definition: The broken remains of an object, usually rock or masonry.
A mass or stratum of fragments of rock lying under the alluvium and derived from the neighbouring rock.
senses.native: 全覆蓋層下、源自鄰近岩石的碎塊層

senses.definition: The whole of the bran of wheat before it is sorted into pollard, bran, etc.
senses.native: 小麥胚芽在分選成糠粉、糠皮等之前的全部部分

examples.text: The building was reduced to rubble.
examples.translation: 該建築已被夷為平地。

examples.text: There is rubble in my garden.
examples.translation: 我的花園裡有廢墟。

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English rouble, rubel, robel, robeil, from Anglo-Norman *robel (“bits of broken stone”). Presumably related to rubbish, originally of same meaning (waste material, bits of stone, rubble). Ultimately presumably from Old Norse rubba (“to huddle, crowd together, heap up", possibly also "to rub, scrape”), from Proto-Germanic *rubbōną (“to rub, scrape”), related to Proto-Germanic *reufaną (“to tear”), *raubōną (“to rob, steal, plunder”), perhaps via Old French robe (English rob
etymology.native: 源於中古英語的 rouble、rubel 等，來自盎格魯 - 諾曼語 *robel（碎塊石）。可能與垃圾同源，最初皆指廢棄物或碎石。最終可能源自古諾斯語 rubba（擁擠堆積），或與原始日耳曼語 *rubbōną（摩擦、刮擦）有關。

senses.definition: Food waste material of any kind.
Useless or disposable material; waste material of any kind.
Specifically, waste material destined not to be reclaimed through recycling, composting, etc.
A place or receptacle for waste material.
Nonsense; gibberish.
Something or someone worthless.
Allocated memory which is no longer in use but has not yet been deallocated.
Data that are misinterpreted as another kind of data.
An easy shot.
Foul, rotten or unripe vegetable matter.
The bowels of an animal; refuse parts of flesh; offal.

senses.definition: The act of breaking.

etymology.text: From Middle English gutted, gotted, equivalent to gut + -ed.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語 gutted, gotted，等同於 gut + -ed。

senses.definition: The act of destroying.

etymology.text: From late Middle English carpette, from Old French carpite, from Medieval Latin carpita or Italian carpita, introduced in the 13th century by the Florentines from the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, from Middle Armenian կարպետ (karpet, “carpet, rug”), earlier կապերտ (kapert).

etymology.text: From late Middle English carpette, from Old French carpite, from Medieval Latin carpita or Italian carpita, introduced in the 13th century by the Florentines from the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, from Middle Armenian կարպետ (karpet, “carpet, rug”), earlier կապերտ (kapert).
etymology.native: 此詞源自13世紀佛羅倫斯人從亞美尼亞的基里西亞王國引入，源自中世紀拉丁語 carpita 或義大利語 carpita，再溯源自古亞美尼亞語 կարպետ（karpet，意為「地毯」），更早為 կապերտ（kapert）。

People sometimes make illogical decisions.

etymology.text: From Middle French superseder (“postpone, defer”), from Latin supersedēre, from super (“over”) + sedēre (“to sit”). The meaning “to replace” is from 1642, probably by association with unrelated precede – note that c instead of s (from cēdere (“to yield”), not sedēre (“to sit”)). As a result, supercede is a common misspelling – see therein for further discussion. Doublet of surcease.
etymology.native: 此詞源於中世紀法語，意為延遲；其「取代」之意約於 1642 年出現，可能與無關之 precede 有關聯。因此，supercede 常被誤寫。

etymology.text: From Middle English belt, from Old English belt (“belt, girdle”), from Proto-West Germanic *baltī̆, from Proto-Germanic *baltijaz (“girdle, belt”), from Latin balteus (“belt, sword-belt”), of Etruscan origin. Cognate with Scots belt (“belt”), Dutch belt, German Balz (“belt”), Danish bælte (“belt”), Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk belte (“belt”), Swedish bälte (“belt, cincture, girdle, zone”), Faroese and Icelandic belti (“belt”).

etymology.text: From Middle English gray, from Old English grǣġ (West Saxon). etymology.text: From Middle English scale, from Latin scāla, usually in plural scālae (“a flight of steps, stairs, staircase, ladder”), for *skand-slā, from scandō (“to climb”); see scan, ascend, descend, etc. Doublet of scala.

senses.definition: simple past and past participle of gild

etymology.native: 來自 gild + -ed。

senses.definition: Having the color or quality of gold.
Made of gold or covered by a thin layer of gold.
Having a falsely pleasant appearance; sugarcoated.

examples.text: Gilded reins do not make for a better horse.
examples.translation: 鑲金的韁繩不會讓馬兒更好。

examples.text: While the rest of us work hard, the robber barons eat with gilded utensils.
examples.translation: 當我們其他人辛苦工作時，強盜貴族卻用鍍金餐具吃飯。

examples.text: The palace was a gilded cage for the princess.

examples.text: Yuri lived in a gilded cage.
examples.translation: 尤莉生活在鑲金牢籠裡。

examples.translation: 外表鑲金香氣四溢，內裡卻腐敗的貴族。

examples.text: Gilded dining rooms.
examples.translation: 鑲金的用餐廳。

etymology.text: From gild + -ed.
etymology.native: 來自 gild + -ed。

senses.definition: Very fine in quality or luxurious.

senses.definition: An element of decoration; that which embellishes or adorns.

Christmas ornament: a Christmas tree decoration.
The articles used in church services.
A characteristic that has a decorative function (typically in order to attract a mate)

examples.text: The bedroom was laden with beautiful ornaments.

examples.text: It is merely an ornament.
examples.translation: 它不過是裝飾而已。

examples.translation: 美國某些地區，火烈鳥雕像是一種受歡迎的草坪裝飾。

examples.text: Oaks, amber, and white wagtails are some of the natural symbols that appear in Latvian ornaments and decorations.
examples.translation: 橡樹、琥珀與白鷺鷥是拉脫維亞飾品與裝飾中出現的自然象徵之一。

relations.native: 一般性的想法、感覺或意識

etymology.text: From Middle English ornament, from Old French ornement, from Latin ornamentum (“equipment, apparatus, furniture, trappings, adornment, embellishment”), from ornāre (“to equip, adorn”). The verb is derived from the noun.

senses.definition: To decorate.

examples.text: We will ornament the windows with trim to make the room seem brighter.
examples.translation: 我們將用邊框裝飾窗戶，讓房間看起來更明亮。

examples.text: Stars ornamented the Christmas tree.
The editor ornamented his plain writing, making it fancier but less clear.

etymology.text: From Middle English ornament, from Old French ornement, from Latin ornamentum (“equipment, apparatus, furniture, trappings, adornment, embellishment”), from ornāre (“to equip, adorn”). The verb is derived from the noun.
etymology.native: 「ornament」源自中世紀英文，來自古法文 ornement，再來自拉丁文 ornamentum（意為裝飾、裝備、飾品），而拉丁文 ornamentum 又來自 ornāre（意為裝飾、裝備）。此動詞源自名詞。

senses.definition: To make more beautiful and attractive by adding ornamentation; to decorate.
To make something sound or look better or more acceptable than it is in reality; to distort, embroider, or even misrepresent or lie.
To enhance by adding something not strictly integral or necessary.
senses.native: 加以裝飾、潤飾，添加非必要的細節

examples.text: Men may embellish their look with gloves or a top hat if they desire.

senses.definition: an adornment (as a bracelet or ring or necklace) made of precious metals and set with gems (or imitation gems)

senses.definition: The act of inviting; solicitation; the requesting of a person's company.

Allurement; enticement.

senses.definition: To cause severe suffering to (stronger than to vex but weaker than to torture.)

examples.text: Bad children love to torment animals.
examples.translation: 壞孩子們喜歡虐待動物。

examples.text: Stop tormenting them.
examples.translation: 別折磨他們了。

examples.translation: 他聽見空無一物中傳來撕心裂肺的哭喊。

examples.text: He was tormented by some deep sorrow.
examples.translation: 他被一種深沉的悲傷所折磨。

etymology.text: From Middle English torment, from Old French torment, from Latin tormentum (“something operated by twisting”), from torquere (“to twist”).
etymology.native: 源自中世紀英文 torment，來自古法文 torment，源自拉丁文 tormentum（意為「被扭轉操作之物」），來自 torquere（意為「扭轉」）

senses.definition: To make angry.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English madden. By surface analysis, mad + -en.

senses.definition: Destroyed, usually in an accident; damaged to the point of unusability.

Very intoxicated from alcohol or recreational drugs.

examples.text: Robbers wrecked the mail train.
examples.translation: 盜匪毀了郵輪。

examples.text: I just wrecked my car in a traffic accident.
examples.translation: 我剛在交通事故中把車毀了。

examples.text: I lost my saber when the ship was wrecked.
examples.translation: 船沉沒時我弄丟了劍。

examples.translation: 醉酒的水手在酒吧裡大鬧一場。

senses.definition: In or to a lower or subordinate position, or a position beneath or below something, physically or figuratively.

etymology.text: From Middle English under, from Old English under, from Proto-West Germanic *undar, from Proto-Germanic *under, from a merger of Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér (“under”) and *h₁entér (“inside”).
etymology.native: 源自中古英語與古英語（under），經原始日耳曼語（*under），由原始印歐語的（*Hn̥dʰér）「在下」與（*h₁entér）「在內」合併而來。

senses.definition: Having been fully removed, including the roots.
Having been removed from a familiar circumstance, especially suddenly and unwillingly.

examples.translation: 那棵白楊樹被連根拔起了。

senses.definition: To put out of place; to disarrange.
To move something, or someone, especially to forcibly move people from their homeland.
To supplant, or take the place of something or someone; to substitute.
To replace, on account of being superior to or more suitable than that which is being replaced.
To have a weight equal to that of the water displaced.
To repress.

etymology.text: From Middle French desplacer (French: déplacer).

senses.definition: The act of displacing, or the state of being displaced; a putting out of place.

The weight of a ship or other floating vessel, traditionally measured or calculated by finding the volume of the vessel below the waterline when afloat, the weight of the displaced liquid being equal to that of the whole displacing body.
Moving the target to avoid an attack; dodging.
A vector quantity which denotes distance with a directional component.
The capability of a communication system to refer to things that are not present (that existed or will exist at another time, or that exist at another location).
The transfer of feelings or emotions from their intended recipient to another object or person.
The amount of liquid displaced by a submerged object.
The transfer of electricity along tubes of induction and thereby polarizing a dielectric.
The process of extracting soluble substances from organic material and the like, whereby a quantity of saturated solvent is displaced, or removed, for another quantity of the solvent.

etymology.text: From Middle English *homles, *hamles, from Old English hāmlēas (“homeless”), equivalent to home + -less. Compare also German heimatlos (“homeless”), Icelandic heimilislaus (“homeless”), West Frisian dakleas (“homeless”, literally “having no roof, roofless”).

senses.definition: In an internal manner; within or inside of external limits; in an inner part or situation.

examples.text: How high is Mount Everest?
examples.translation: 珠穆朗瑪峰有多高？

Searching through a sample for a target; an act of screening, or the method for it.

etymology.text: From Middle English scren, screne (“windscreen, firescreen”), from Anglo-Norman escren (“firescreen, the tester of a bed”), Old French escren, escrein, escran (modern French écran (“screen”)), from Middle Dutch scherm, from Old Dutch skirm, from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi, from Proto-Germanic *skirmiz (“fur, shelter, covering, screen”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut, divide”).
etymology.native: 「螢幕」一詞源於中古英語的 scren，其後可追溯至盎格魯諾曼語、古法語及中低地德語。

senses.definition: To filter by passing through a screen.
To filter.
To shelter or conceal.
To remove information, or censor intellectual material from viewing. To hide the facts.
senses.native: 刪除資訊或審查知識內容，使人無法閱覽；掩蓋事實

senses.definition: To present publicly (on the screen).
To fit with a screen.

senses.definition: To search chemical libraries by means of a computational technique in order to identify chemical compounds which would potentially bind to a given biological target such as a protein.
senses.native: 以計算方法篩選化合物資料庫，找出可能與某生物標的（如蛋白質）結合的化合物（虛擬篩選）

senses.definition: To stand so as to block a defender from reaching a teammate.
senses.native: （籃球）設掩護，阻擋防守者接近隊友（掩護）

senses.definition: To determine the source or subject matter of a call before deciding whether to answer the phone.

etymology.text: From Middle English scren, screne (“windscreen, firescreen”), from Anglo-Norman escren (“firescreen, the tester of a bed”), Old French escren, escrein, escran (modern French écran (“screen”)), from Middle Dutch scherm, from Old Dutch skirm, from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi, from Proto-Germanic *skirmiz (“fur, shelter, covering, screen”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut, divide”).
etymology.native: 「螢幕」一詞源於中古英語的 scren，其後可追溯至盎格魯諾曼語、古法語及中低地德語。

senses.definition: A curtailment or reduction.
An act of reducing expenses; economizing.
An act of terminating the employment of a worker or making an employee redundant, often to reduce expenses; a layoff.
Withdrawal.
The adoption of a defensive and hostile posture; refusal to compromise, radicalization.
A defensive work constructed within a fortification to make it more defensible by allowing defenders to retreat into and fight from it even after the enemy has taken the outer work.

examples.text: Rugged and ascending with short abrupt turns this road was blocked at every uncovered point with abbattis and small retrenchments.

senses.definition: The study of money, currency and trade, and the efficient use of resources.

Frugal use of resources.
The method of divine government of the world. (See Economy (religion) on Wikipedia.Wikipedia )
The part of a commercial passenger airplane or train reserved for those paying the lower standard fares; economy class.
The regular operation of nature in the generation, nutrition and preservation of animals or plants.
System of management; general regulation and disposition of the affairs of a state or nation, or of any department of government.
A system of rules, regulations, rites and ceremonies.
The disposition or arrangement of any work.
Management of one’s residency.

etymology.text: From Middle English yconomye, yconomy, borrowed via Old French yconomie or Medieval Latin from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νέμω (némō, “distribute, allocate”). By surface analysis, eco- + -nomy. The first recorded sense of the word economy, found in a work possibly composed in 1440, is “the management of economic affairs”, in this case, of a monastery.
etymology.native: 源自中古英語（yconomye、yconomy），經由古法語（yconomie）或中世紀拉丁語借自拉丁語（oeconomia），來自古希臘語（οἰκονομία）「家務管理、行政」，由（οἶκος）「家」加（νέμω）「分配」組成。表面分析為（eco-）加（-nomy）。最早的詞義見於約 1440 年的作品，指「經濟事務的管理」，在此指修道院的事務。

senses.definition: An amount by which a quantity decreases or is decreased.
