examples.translation: 祝你們有快樂的一週。

examples.text: He is a pleasant person.
examples.translation: 他是個好脾氣的人。

examples.text: Have a pleasant trip.
examples.translation: 祝你一路上玩得愉快。

examples.text: She had a pleasant dream last night.
examples.translation: 她昨晚做了個美夢。

examples.text: His voice is pleasant to listen to.
examples.translation: 他的聲音很悅耳。

etymology.text: From Middle English plesaunte, from Old French plaisant. By surface analysis, please + -ant. Related to Dutch plezant (“full of fun or pleasure”). Partly displaced Old English wynsum, which became Modern English winsome.

senses.definition: Awfully; dreadfully; terribly.
Very, extremely.

examples.text: That's an awful big house.
She seemed awful nice when I met her yesterday.
He was blubbering away something awful.

etymology.text: From Middle English agheful, awfull, auful, aȝefull, equivalent to awe + -ful. Compare Old English eġeful, eġefull (“terrifying; awful”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to statistics.

examples.text: Officials like statistical evasion.
Ignoring endogeneity leads to a bad statistical model.
Probit statistical models can be used for binary variables.
In this semester, students study and apply statistical sampling techniques.
This kind of case is amenable to statistical treatment.
We've hired number crunchers to do the statistical analysis.

relations.native: 人口普查、人口調查、戶口檢查

etymology.text: From statistic + -al.

senses.definition: At the present time; in the current era.
in these times

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: Nowadays many people travel by car.
examples.translation: 現在很多人開車去旅行。

examples.text: I almost never watch TV nowadays.
examples.translation: 現在我幾乎不看電視。

examples.text: Nowadays many women have a job.
examples.translation: 現代很多女生有份工作。

examples.text: Meat is expensive nowadays.
examples.translation: 如今肉類價格昂貴。

examples.text: Nowadays mobile phones are very popular.
examples.translation: 現今手機非常普及。

examples.text: Nowadays, almost every home has one or two televisions.
examples.translation: 現在幾乎每家每戶也有一兩台電視機了。

etymology.text: From now + adays.

senses.definition: To pay heed to; notice; to take notice of, to perceive.
To express in words or writing; to state, as an observation.
To make a remark or remarks on, to comment on (something).
To pass comment on (something); to indicate, point out.
To mark (someone or something) out; to distinguish, to make notable.

examples.text: Everyone remarked on his new hairstyle.
Peter remarked that the pudding was too sweet.
I remarked a certain twang in his southern pronunciation.
He remarked that it was getting late.

etymology.text: From Middle French remarquer, from Old French remarquer, from re- (“again”) + marquer (“to mark”), equivalent to re- (“again”) + mark.

senses.definition: A course of action that a person intends to follow.
A goal or purpose.
A process of the healing of a wound.
Tension; straining, stretching.
A stretching or bending of the mind toward an object or a purpose (an intent); closeness of application; fixedness of attention; earnestness.
The object toward which the thoughts are directed; end; aim.
Any mental apprehension of an object.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: I have no intention of resigning.
examples.translation: 我無意辭職。

examples.text: It wasn't my intention.
examples.translation: 那不是我的本意。

examples.text: That wasn't my intention.
examples.translation: 那不是我故意的。

examples.text: I have no intention of telling you the result.
examples.translation: 我並不打算把結果告訴你。

examples.text: You shouldn't forget your original intentions.
examples.translation: 不能忘記自己的初衷。

examples.text: Tom has no intention of going to Mary's wedding.
examples.translation: 湯姆不打算去參加瑪麗的婚禮。

etymology.text: From Middle English entencioun, intention, from Old French entencion, from Latin intentiō, intentiōnem. Compare intent. Equivalent to intent + -ion.

senses.definition: Occurring at the same time.

examples.text: Tom and Mary answered simultaneously.
Both of them resigned simultaneously.
Everything happened simultaneously.
It's simultaneously getting worse and better.
Gustavo can do several things simultaneously.
Every Tatoeba member is simultaneously student and teacher.

etymology.text: From simultaneous + -ly.

senses.definition: To confer with others in order to come to terms or reach an agreement.
To arrange or settle something by mutual agreement.
To succeed in coping with, getting over or navigate a hazard or obstacle.
To transfer to another person with all the rights of the original holder; to pass, as a bill.
To transact business; to carry on trade.
To intrigue; to scheme.

examples.text: Gustavo suggested negotiating with the aliens.
Algeria doesn't negotiate with terrorists.
The diplomats are meeting to negotiate.
She then proceeded to negotiate with her bank.
His job is to negotiate with foreign buyers.
The government of Mexico refused to negotiate.

etymology.text: c. 1598; borrowed from Latin negōtiātus, perfect active participle of negōtior (“to do business, trade”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from negotium (“business”) + -or, from nec (“not”) + otium (“leisure, ease, inactivity”).

senses.definition: The process of achieving agreement through discussion.

examples.text: The negotiation is off.
examples.translation: 談判中止了。

examples.text: Both countries entered into peace negotiations.
Algeria wasn't invited to the negotiations.
We have agreed to continue the negotiations.
We held many negotiations but to no purpose.
The peace negotiations will start this week.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Middle French négociation, or from Latin negotiatio (“the carrying on of business, a wholesale business”), from negotiari (“to carry on business”). By surface analysis, negotiate + -ion.

senses.definition: Concise, brief, or presented in a condensed form; presenting information in such a form.
Performed speedily, without formal ceremony, and (especially) without regard to legality.
Performed by omitting the procedures of a full trial, but within a legally valid framework.

examples.text: A summary review is in the appendix.
They used summary executions to break the resistance of the people.
The matter was brought to a close by summary dismissal of the cases.
The summary executions caused outrage.

etymology.text: From Middle English summary, from Medieval Latin summārius, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives).

senses.definition: Determination; will power.
A determination to do something; a fixed decision.
An act of resolving something; resolution.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: You inspire others through your quiet resolve.

etymology.text: From Middle English resolven, from Old French resolver, a learned borrowing of Latin resolvō (“loosen, thaw, melt, resolve”), equivalent to re- + solve. Piecewise doublet of re-solve.

senses.definition: Used as a positive response to good news or information.

examples.text: They're making a sequel? Ah, sweet!

etymology.text: From Middle English soot, sweete, swete, swoote, from Old English swēte, swoete, swōt, swœ̄te (“sweet”), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtī, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz (“sweet”), from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus (“sweet”), from *sweh₂d- (“sweet”) + *-us.

senses.definition: The basic taste sensation induced by sugar.
A confection made from sugar, or high in sugar content; a candy.
A food eaten for dessert.
Synonym of sweetheart, a term of affection.
That which is sweet or pleasant in odour; a perfume.
Sweetness, delight; something pleasant to the mind or senses.

examples.text: Share out the sweets between you.
examples.translation: 你們分了這些糖果吧。

examples.text: I want something sweet to eat.
examples.translation: 我想要吃甜的東西。

examples.text: This music has something in itself, which fills my heart with sweet melancholy.

etymology.text: From Middle English soot, sweete, swete, swoote, from Old English swēte, swoete, swōt, swœ̄te (“sweet”), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtī, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz (“sweet”), from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus (“sweet”), from *sweh₂d- (“sweet”) + *-us.

senses.definition: A strong desire to do something.

examples.text: Advertisements urge us to buy luxuries.
examples.translation: 廣告慫恿我們買奢侈品。

examples.text: I urge you to tell him the truth.
examples.translation: 我勸你告訴他實話。

examples.text: You should try to resist the urge to do that.
I urge you to read the contract carefully.
I've been trying to resist the urge to do that.
I had an urge to eat an authentic pretzel!

etymology.text: From Latin urgeō (“urge”).

senses.definition: To press; to push; to drive; to impel; to force onward.
To put mental pressure on; to ply with motives, arguments, persuasion, or importunity.
To provoke; to exasperate.
To press hard upon; to follow closely.
To present in an urgent manner; to insist upon.
To press onward or forward.
To be pressing in argument; to insist; to persist.
To treat with forcible means; to take severe or violent measures with.

examples.text: Tobias urged everyone to be careful.
Tom urged Mary to drive carefully.
The kids urged their father to leave quickly.
The doctor urged the patient to stop smoking.
Hunger urged him to steal.
examples.translation: 飢餓促使他偷竊。

examples.text: Jessie urged the little donkey forward.
examples.translation: 傑西鞭策小毛驢前進。

relations.native: 按壓（按鍵或按鈕）後放開，使其啟動

etymology.text: From Latin urgeō (“urge”).

senses.definition: To sense a smell or smells.
To detect or perceive; often with out.
Followed by like or of if descriptive: to have a particular smell, whether good or bad.
To smell of; to have a smell of
To smell bad; to stink.
To have a particular tincture or smack of any quality; to savour.
To give heed to.

examples.text: Do you even know how to smell the flowers?
examples.translation: 你還知道花聞起來是怎樣的嗎？

examples.text: You smell it. Do five spice tea eggs smell good?
examples.translation: 你聞聞香味，五香茶葉蛋香不香？

examples.text: "It smells like popcorn." "You're right!"
examples.translation: 「聞起來像爆米花。」「你說的對！」

examples.text: I could smell the alcohol on his breath.
examples.translation: 我能聞到他呼吸中的酒精味。

examples.text: It's been said that one should not smell deer musk when pregnant.
examples.translation: 據說懷孕的時候不能聞麝香。

examples.text: Among all cheeses, the one that I like is Camembert. I love its smell because it makes me nostalgic.

relations.native: 散發出強烈且令人不悅的氣味

etymology.text: From Middle English smellen, smillen, smyllen, smullen, from Old English *smyllan, *smiellan (“to smell, emit fumes”), from Proto-West Germanic *smallijan (“to glow, burn, smoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *smel- (“to burn, smoke, smoulder; tar, pitch”). The noun is from Middle English smel, smil, smul (“smell, odour”). Related to Saterland Frisian smeele (“to smoulder”), Middle Dutch smōlen (“to burn, smoulder”) (whence Dutch smeulen (“to smoulder”)), Middle Low German smölen (“to be hazy, b

senses.definition: An instance of sniffing.
A quantity of something that is inhaled through the nose.
A brief perception, or tiny amount.
Cocaine.
A toddler or young child.

etymology.text: From Middle English sniffen, of imitative origin.

senses.definition: To express (an action, thought or idea) by means of particular words.
To perform (a passage) with a particular phrasing.
To divide into melodic phrases.

examples.text: Sorry, my question was phrased incorrectly.
"Call up" is a phrase that means to telephone.
I wonder what this phrase means.
examples.translation: 我想知道這句話的意思。

examples.text: I wasn't sure how to phrase my condolences without sounding patronising.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).

senses.definition: An individual or organization that creates goods and services.
One who produces an artistic production, such as an album, a theater production, a film, a TV program, a video game, and so on.
An organism that produces complex organic compounds from simple molecules and an external source of energy.
An arrest for speeding after which the driver is allowed seven (in the UK) or ten (in Ireland) days to produce his/her driving licence and related documents at a police station.
A furnace for producing combustible gas for fuel.

examples.text: Tom Jackson is the supervising producer.
Daniel told the producer about Jessica.
Jonas is a television producer.
Algeria is one of Africa's top oil producers.
Daniel heard Amanda's talk with the producer.
He left the producer a message on voice mail.

etymology.text: From produce + -er.

senses.definition: A simple aliphatic alcohol formally derived from ethane by replacing one hydrogen atom with a hydroxyl group: CH₃-CH₂-OH.
Specifically, this form of alcohol as a fuel.

examples.text: The price of ethanol fell.
It's the ethanol in beer that makes you drunk.
The government is supporting the development of ethanol production.
Ethanol is an alcohol.
Methanol is far more toxic than ethanol.

etymology.text: Contracted from ethyl + alcohol. Ethyl is from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “ether”), influenced by German Äthyl. May be decomposed as ethane + -ol.

senses.definition: In a typical or common manner.
In an expected or customary manner.

examples.text: Today is another typically hectic day.
She typically entered the house early.
Vertebrates typically have teeth.
It's a restaurant with typically Finnish food.
A truck typically uses more gas than a car.
An SUV typically uses more gas than a car.

etymology.text: From typical + -ly.

senses.definition: To act before (someone), especially to prevent an action.
To take up or introduce (something) prematurely.
To know of (something) before it happens; to expect.
To eagerly wait for (something)

examples.text: More difficult than anyone had anticipated.
The attendants anticipated all our needs.
I should have anticipated this happening.
We do not anticipate their buying a new car.
examples.translation: 我們認為他們不會買新車。

examples.text: I anticipate that there will be trouble.
examples.translation: 我預料會有麻煩。

examples.text: I couldn't anticipate that that would happen.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin anticipātus, perfect passive participle of anticipō (“to anticipate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ante- (“before”), + capiō (“to take”, cip- when prefixed) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See capable.

senses.definition: The sound of laughing, produced by air so expelled; any similar sound.

A movement (usually involuntary) of the muscles of the laughing face, particularly of the lips, and of the whole body, with a peculiar expression of the eyes, indicating merriment, satisfaction or derision, and usually attended by a sonorous and interrupted expulsion of air from the lungs.
A reason for merriment.

examples.text: Laughter is good for your health.
examples.translation: 笑一笑，十年少。

examples.text: I'm dying of laughter.
examples.translation: 笑死我了！

examples.text: His words set everybody roaring with laughter.
examples.translation: 他的話把大家惹得哈哈大笑。

examples.text: The whole audience erupted in laughter.
examples.translation: 鬨堂大笑。

examples.text: A day without laughter is a day wasted.
examples.translation: 沒有笑聲的一天肯定是最為虛度的一天。

examples.text: Is laughter a quality of man only?
examples.translation: 笑是人類特有的嗎？

etymology.text: From Middle English laughter, laghter, laȝter, from Old English hleahtor (“laughter, jubilation, derision”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *klek-, *kleg- (“to shout”). Cognate with German Gelächter (“laughter, hilarity, merriment”), Danish and Norwegian latter (“laughter”), Icelandic hlátur (“laughter”). More at laugh.

senses.definition: To poke or strike with the knee.
To move on the knees; to use the knees to move.
To kneel to.

examples.text: She kneed me again, not even caring that she was hurt.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English kne, from Old English cnēow, from Proto-West Germanic *kneu, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéw-o-m, a thematic derivative of *ǵónu.

senses.definition: Very large.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: Giant pandas live only in China.
examples.translation: 大熊貓只住在中國裡。

examples.text: Humans worshipped giant alien creatures.
I've never seen such a giant watermelon!
examples.translation: 我從沒見過那麼大的西瓜！

examples.text: The giant creature pushed the tree over.
examples.translation: 巨大的生物把樹推倒了。`

examples.text: Seen from the sky, this river looks like a giant snake.
examples.translation: 從天上看下來，這條河像一條巨蛇。

examples.text: There will be a giant crop of corn this year.

etymology.text: From Middle English geaunt, geant, from Old French geant, gaiant (Modern French géant) from Vulgar Latin *gagās, gagant-, from Latin gigās, gigant-, from Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”). Cognate to giga- (“1,000,000,000”). Largely Displaced native Old English ent (“giant”), Old English eoten (“giant or jötunn”), and Old English þyrs (“giant or ogre”). Compare English ent (“giant tree-man”), ettin (“giant or troll”) and thurse (“giant”).

senses.definition: A logic gate that implements material implication.

examples.text: What do his words imply?
examples.translation: 他的話暗示著什麼？

etymology.text: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.

senses.definition: A domesticated subspecies of red junglefowl (Gallus gallus domesticus).
The meat from this bird eaten as food.
A young, attractive, slim man, usually having little body hair; compare chickenhawk.
The game of dare.

A confrontational game in which the participants move toward each other at high speed (usually in automobiles); the player who turns first to avoid colliding into the other is the "chicken" (that is, the loser).
A simple dance in which the movements of a chicken are imitated.
A coward.
A young or inexperienced person.
A kilogram of cocaine.
The young of any bird; a chick.
A small pewter pot used in a tavern.

examples.text: I'd like three pounds of chicken.
examples.translation: 我要三磅的雞肉。

examples.text: Don't forget to buy chicken.
examples.translation: 別忘記買雞肉。

examples.text: The chicken is undercooked.
examples.translation: 雞肉還不夠熟。

examples.text: We had some chicken soup.
examples.translation: 我們喝了些雞湯。

examples.text: That meat is chicken.
examples.translation: 那個肉是雞肉。

examples.text: We have two dogs, three cats, and six chickens.
examples.translation: 我們養了兩隻狗、三隻貓和六隻雞。

etymology.text: From Middle English chiken (also as chike > English chick), from Old English ċicen, ċycen (“chicken”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *kiukīn (“chicken”), or alternatively from Proto-West Germanic *kukkīn, equivalent to cock + -en.

senses.definition: Cowardly.

examples.text: This meat is chicken.
examples.translation: 這是雞肉。

etymology.text: From Middle English chiken (also as chike > English chick), from Old English ċicen, ċycen (“chicken”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *kiukīn (“chicken”), or alternatively from Proto-West Germanic *kukkīn, equivalent to cock + -en.

senses.definition: To avoid a situation one is afraid of.

examples.text: He chickened out.
examples.translation: 他臨陣退縮了。

etymology.text: From Middle English chiken (also as chike > English chick), from Old English ċicen, ċycen (“chicken”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *kiukīn (“chicken”), or alternatively from Proto-West Germanic *kukkīn, equivalent to cock + -en.

senses.definition: A crime or sin.
An affront, injury, or insult.
The state of being offended or displeased; anger; displeasure.
A strategy and tactics employed when in position to score; contrasted with defense.
The portion of a team dedicated to scoring when in position to do so; contrasted with defense.

examples.text: Do you know about Tom's offense?
I'm sure Tom meant no offense.
She took offense at something.
She took offense at her daughter's behavior.
He likes to flout rules he takes offense to.
He took offense at his daughter's behavior.

etymology.text: From Middle English offence, from Old French offense, from Latin offensa (“a striking against; displeasure; injury”).

senses.definition: Not excessive; acting in moderation.
More than mild but less than severe.
Mediocre.
Average or middling, for example in price.
Not violent or rigorous; temperate; mild; gentle.
Having an intermediate position between liberal and conservative.

examples.text: Moderate exercise will do you good.
Moderate exercise is good for you.
Try to be moderate in drinking.
Moderate exercise is necessary for good health.
examples.translation: 適度運動對身體健康是必要的。

examples.text: Algerians practice a moderate form of Islam.
Taking moderate exercise will keep you healthy.

etymology.text: From Middle English moderat(e) (“moderate, temperate”), borrowed from Latin moderātus, perfect active participle of moderor (“to regulate, to restrain, to moderate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from moder-, modes-, a stem appearing also in modestus (“moderate, discreet, modest”), from modus (“a measure”); see mode and modest. Doublet of moderato. Displaced native Old English ġemetlīċ (“moderate”) and metegian (“to moderate”). Cognate with French modéré.

senses.definition: One who holds an intermediate position between extremes, as in politics.

One of a party in Scottish Church history dominant in the 18th century, lax in doctrine and discipline, but intolerant of evangelicalism and popular rights. It caused the secessions of 1733 and 1761, and its final resultant was the Disruption of 1843.

examples.text: The moderates are the natural advocates of ecumenism against the fanatics of their churches.

etymology.text: From Middle English moderat(e) (“moderate, temperate”), borrowed from Latin moderātus, perfect active participle of moderor (“to regulate, to restrain, to moderate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from moder-, modes-, a stem appearing also in modestus (“moderate, discreet, modest”), from modus (“a measure”); see mode and modest. Doublet of moderato. Displaced native Old English ġemetlīċ (“moderate”) and metegian (“to moderate”). Cognate with French modéré.

senses.definition: A spy operating abroad illegally and under non-official cover, without visible ties to his or her country’s authorities.
Contraband, esp. illegal substances such as drugs.
An illegal act or technique.

examples.text: Prostitution, gambling, the use of narcotic substances, drunkenness, disorder, and all other illegal activities are STRICTLY FORBIDDEN.
examples.translation: 嚴禁賣淫嫖娼，賭博，吸毒，酗酒滋事等違法犯罪活動！

examples.text: Russia started its illegal and unjustifiable war of aggression against Ukraine, and Russia can end it.
examples.translation: 俄羅斯對烏克蘭發動了非法、不公義的侵略戰爭，而俄羅斯應該終止這一切。

etymology.text: Borrowed from French illégal, from Medieval Latin illegalis, from Latin legalis, by surface analysis, il- + legal. In senses relating to immigration, via clipping of illegal alien or illegal immigrant.

senses.definition: Myself, oneself.
Himself, herself, itself, themself, themselves; that specific (person mentioned).

examples.text: This argument was put forward by the defendant self.

etymology.text: From Middle English salve, self, silf, from Old English self, seolf, sylf, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”).

senses.definition: One individual's personality, character, demeanor, or disposition.
The subject of one's own experience of phenomena: perception, emotions, thoughts.
An individual person as the object of the person's own reflective consciousness (plural selves).
Self-interest or personal advantage.
A seedling produced by self-pollination (plural selfs).
A flower having its colour uniform as opposed to variegated.
Any molecule, cell, or tissue of an organism's own (belonging to the self), as opposed to a foreign (nonself) molecule, cell, or tissue (for example, infective, allogenic, or xenogenic).

examples.text: It doesn't matter how others see you. What is important is to be sure to affirm your own self.
examples.translation: 別人怎樣看自己不重要,重要的是要保證自己得到自己的認同。

examples.text: One's own self.

etymology.text: From Middle English salve, self, silf, from Old English self, seolf, sylf, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”).

senses.definition: The achievement of political, social or economic power by an individual or group.
The process of supporting another person or persons to discover and claim personal power.
The state of being empowered (either generally, or specifically).
Government programs encouraging advancement of blacks.

examples.text: Empowerment of girls is a major theme in movies today.
I read a quote about self empowerment or self love every day for inspiration.
The first step to self empowerment is to believe that you are good even with your flaws.
Stereotypical beliefs about femininity hinder women's empowerment and limit their opportunities for growth.

etymology.text: From empower + -ment.

senses.definition: Equal to or fulfilling some requirement.

examples.text: This meal is adequate for three.
examples.translation: 這飯足夠三個人吃。

examples.text: He is adequate for the post.
We need not only adequate water but clean water.
examples.translation: 我們不僅需要充足的水，還需要乾淨的水。

examples.text: The pay is not adequate for a family of six.
He took adequate clothes for a weekend trip.
The national health service was far from adequate.

etymology.text: Learned borrowing from Latin adaequātus, perfect passive participle of adaequō (“to make equal to”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from ad (“to, towards, at”) + aequō (“to make equal, equalize”), from aequus (“equal”). Cognate with French adéquat. By surface analysis, ad- + equate.

senses.definition: A sufficient amount of; enough.

examples.text: We have adequate money for the journey.

etymology.text: Learned borrowing from Latin adaequātus, perfect passive participle of adaequō (“to make equal to”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from ad (“to, towards, at”) + aequō (“to make equal, equalize”), from aequus (“equal”). etymology.text: From Old English port, borrowed from Latin portus (“port, harbour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”) (and thus a distant doublet of ford). The directional sense, attested since at least the 1500s, derives from ancient vessels with the steering oar on the right (see etymology of starboard), which therefore had to moor with their left sides facing the dock or wharf. Doublet of fjard, fjord, firth, ford, and Portus.

examples.translation: 湯姆的航班延誤了，然後被取消了。

examples.text: He canceled the appointment at the last moment.
examples.translation: 他到了最後的一刻才取消了約會。

etymology.text: From Middle English cancellen, from Anglo-Norman canceler (“to cross out with lines”) (modern French chanceler (“to stagger, sway”)), from Old French canceler, from Latin cancellō (“to make resemble a lattice”), from cancellus (“a railing or lattice”), diminutive of cancer (“a lattice”).

senses.definition: To schedule again or at a different time.
To reclassify; to change the schedule (division into which something is classified) of.

Can we reschedule the appointment next week?

etymology.text: From re- + schedule.

senses.definition: One who opposes another; one who works or takes a position against someone or something; one who attempts to stop the progress of someone or something.
One who opposes another physically (in a fight, sport, game, or competition).
One who opposes another in words (in a dispute, argument or controversy).
One who is opposed or objects (to a policy, course of action or set of ideas).
The participant who opens an academic debate by putting forward objections to a theological or philosophical thesis.

examples.text: Our team defeated our opponent 5-4.
examples.translation: 我們這隊5-4擊敗對手。

examples.text: He knocked his opponent out.
examples.translation: 他把對手擊倒了。

examples.text: I knocked out my opponents.

examples.text: The home team always have an advantage over their opponents.
examples.translation: 主場隊總是比對手有優勢。

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin oppōnēns (“opposing”), present active participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”).

senses.definition: Opposing; adverse; antagonistic.
Situated in front; opposite.

examples.text: Opponent (or opposing) armies.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin oppōnēns (“opposing”), present active participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”).

senses.definition: An act of hitting; a blow, a hit.
An act of striking with a weapon; a blow.
A single movement with a tool; also, an impact of a tool on an object.
The hitting of a bell or similar by the clapper or hammer of a clock; the sound thereof; the time when this occurs.
The action of hitting the ball with the bat; a shot.
A single act of striking at the ball with a club; also, at matchplay, a shot deducted from a player's score at a hole as a result of a handicapping system.
A point awarded to a player in case of interference or obstruction by the opponent.
The hitting of a ball with a racket; also, the movement of the racket and arm that produces that impact.
One of a series of beats or movements against a resisting medium, by means of which movement through or upon it is accomplished.

The movement of an oar or paddle through water: either the cycle of movement as a whole, or the propelling phase (as opposed to the return); the manner in which such movements are made; a rowing style.
The rower nearest the stern of the boat, the movement of whose oar sets the rhythm for the other rowers; the position in the boat occupied by this rower.
A movement of the arms and legs which propels a swimmer through the water; a specific combination of such movements, constituting a swimming style.
A beat or throb, as of the heart or pulse.
A single movement or thrust of a reciprocating device (such as a piston or connecting rod).
The length of this movement.
A thrust of the penis during sexual intercourse.
An act causing hurt or death, especially when seen as divine punishment.
A damaging occurrence, especially if sudden; a blow, a calamity.
An amount of work; specifically, a large amount of business or work.
A powerful or sudden effort by which something is done or produced; also, something accomplished by such an effort; an achievement, a feat.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

etymology.text: The noun is derived from Middle English strok, stroke (“blow from a weapon, cut”), from Old English strāc, from Proto-West Germanic *straik, from Proto-Germanic *straikaz (“stroke”), from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to rub, stroke; to shear; to strike”).

senses.definition: The legal dissolution of a marriage.
A separation of connected things.
The separation of a bonded pair of animals.
That which separates.

examples.translation: 我聽說瑪麗想離婚。

examples.text: The root cause of any divorce is marriage.
examples.translation: 結婚是所有離婚的主要原因。

examples.text: Marriage is the main cause of divorce.
examples.translation: 婚姻是造成離婚的主因。

examples.text: I'm seriously considering filing for divorce.

etymology.text: Derived from Old French divorce, from Latin dīvortium, from dīvertere (“to turn aside”), from dī- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

senses.definition: Inclination towards something.
The diagonal line between warp and weft in a woven fabric.
A wedge-shaped piece of cloth taken out of a garment (such as the waist of a dress) to diminish its circumference.
A voltage or current applied to an electronic device, such as a transistor electrode, to move its operating point to a desired part of its transfer function.
The difference between the expectation of the sample estimator and the true population value, which reduces the representativeness of the estimator by systematically distorting it.

In the games of crown green bowls and lawn bowls: a weight added to one side of a bowl so that as it rolls, it will follow a curved rather than a straight path; the oblique line followed by such a bowl; the lopsided shape or structure of such a bowl. A person's favourite member of a K-pop band.

pronunciations.attribution: Self, recorded using the program Shtooka.

examples.text: People tend to look at others with bias.

etymology.text: c. 1520 in the sense "oblique line". As a technical term in the game of bowls c. 1560, whence the figurative use (c. 1570).

senses.definition: A likelihood of behaving in a particular way or going in a particular direction; a tending toward.
An organised unit or faction within a larger political organisation.

examples.text: He has a tendency to Whiggishness.
She has a tendency to fantasise.
You have the tendency to forget.

etymology.text: From Medieval Latin tendentia, from tendens, present participle of tendō.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, produced by, operated with, or utilising electricity; electrical.
Of or relating to an electronic version of a musical instrument that has an acoustic equivalent.
Emotionally thrilling; electrifying.

examples.text: This factory manufactures electric stoves.
examples.translation: 這家工廠生產電爐。

examples.text: My brother bought an electric guitar.
examples.translation: 我的兄弟買了電子吉他。

examples.text: My father is an electric engineer.
examples.translation: 我父親是個電子工程師。

examples.text: I've bought an electric bicycle.
examples.translation: 我買了一輛電動腳踏車。

examples.text: It's warm, so I turned on the electric fan.
examples.translation: 天氣熱，我就把電風扇打開了。

examples.text: My favourite musical instrument is the electric guitar.
examples.translation: 我最喜歡的樂器是電吉他。

etymology.text: First attested in c. 1646 in a publication by Thomas Browne. From New Latin ēlectricus (“electrical; of amber”), from ēlectr(um) (“amber”) + -icus (“adjectival suffix”); from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”); related to ἠλέκτωρ (ēléktōr, “shining sun”), of unknown origin (see which for more). The Latin term was apparently used first with the sense electrical in 1600 by the English physician and scientist William Gilbert in his work De Magnete.

senses.definition: To step quickly and heavily, once or repeatedly.
To move (the foot or feet) quickly and heavily, once or repeatedly.
To strike, beat, or press forcibly with the bottom of the foot, or by thrusting the foot downward.
To mark by pressing quickly and heavily.
To give an official marking to, generally by impressing or imprinting a design or symbol.
To apply postage stamps to.
To mark; to impress.

etymology.text: From Middle English stampen (“to pound, crush”), from assumed Old English *stampian, variant of Old English stempan (“to crush, pound, pound in mortar, stamp”), from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, *stampijan, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną, *stampijaną (“to trample, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *stemb- (“to trample down”).

senses.definition: Involving extreme force or motion.
Involving physical conflict.
Likely to use physical force.
Intensely vivid.
Produced or effected by force; not spontaneous; unnatural.
Acute, extreme, sharp.

George Orwell was a violent antifascist.
Violent clashes broke out in Mariupol.
She's violent right now. It'd be better to avoid her.
examples.translation: 她現在很暴力。最好避著點。

examples.translation: 我們不夠強硬。

etymology.text: From Middle English violent, from Old French violent, from Latin violentus, from vīs (“strength”). Displaced native Old English stræc. For the verb, compare French violenter.

senses.definition: To be impelled or driven forward by the action of wind upon sails, as a ship on water; to be impelled on a body of water by steam or other power.
To move through or on the water; to swim, as a fish or a waterfowl.
To ride in a boat, especially a sailboat.
To set sail; to begin a voyage.
To move briskly and gracefully through the air.
To move briskly but sedately.
To deal out (cards) from a distance by impelling them across a surface.

examples.text: I saw a white cloud sailing across the sky.
examples.translation: 我見到一片白雲在空中飄過。

etymology.text: From Middle English saile, sayle, seil, seyl, from Old English seġl, from Proto-West Germanic *segl, from Proto-Germanic *seglą. Cognate with West Frisian seil, Low German Segel, Dutch zeil, German Segel, Danish sejl, Swedish segel.

senses.definition: As a result or consequence of something; subsequently.
subsequently, following after in time or sequence.

examples.text: It looks consequently bigger.

Often with up, to speed up the rate of doing something.
To cause to be done quickly.
To hasten; to impel to greater speed; to urge on.
To impel to precipitate or thoughtless action; to urge to confused or irregular activity.
To put: to convey coal in the mine, e.g. from the working to the tramway.

examples.text: Hurry up, Martin. We're already late!
examples.translation: 快點，馬丁。我們已經遲到了！

examples.translation: 我匆匆忙忙的趕到那房子去，但卻發現裡面原來是空的。

examples.text: I hurried in order to catch the first train.
examples.translation: 我匆匆忙忙，為的是能趕上第一班火車。

etymology.text: From Middle English horien (“to rush, impel”), probably a variation of hurren (“to vibrate rapidly, buzz”), from Proto-Germanic *hurzaną (“to rush”) (compare Middle High German hurren (“to hasten”), Norwegian hurre (“to whirl around”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”) (compare Latin currō (“to run”), Tocharian A kursär/Tocharian B kwarsär (“league; course”)). Related to hurr, horse, rush.

senses.definition: A system of rules and principles for the structure of a language, or of languages in general.

Actual or presumed prescriptive notions about the correct use of a language.
A book describing the grammar (noun sense 1 or noun sense 2) of a language.

Displaced native Old English stæfcræft; a doublet of glamour, glamoury, gramarye, and grimoire. Piecewise doublet of grammatic.

senses.definition: Not breaching any constraints of the grammar, or morpho-syntax, of the relevant language.

A rapid reduction in asset prices due to broad efforts to raise cash in anticipation of such prices continuing to decline.
A highly amusing or entertaining performer, performance, or show; a riot, a scream.
Foxtail millet or Italian millet (Setaria italica), the second-most widely grown species of millet.
A plant of the genus Panicum, or of similar plants of other genera (especially Echinochloa and Setaria) formerly included within Panicum; panicgrass or panic grass.
The edible grain obtained from one of the above plants.

etymology.text: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French panique, a word itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, “pertaining to Pan”); Pan, the Greek god of fields and woods, was believed to be the source of mysterious sounds that caused contagious, groundless fear in herds and crowds, or in people in lonely spots.

senses.definition: to give one's time, focus one's efforts, commit oneself, etc. entirely for, on, or to a certain matter; to consecrate.

examples.text: Uranus hasn't been adequately probed.
Everyone should prepare adequately.
I've been adequately punished.
You must be adequately prepared.
I don't know how to adequately express what a fantastic person you are.
It's almost impossible to speak this language adequately well because its inflections are very irregular.

etymology.text: From adequate + -ly.

senses.definition: Something that constrains; a restriction.
An irresistible force or compulsion.
The repression of one's feelings.
A condition that a solution to an optimization problem must satisfy.
A linkage or other restriction that maintains database integrity.

Following the rules was a constraint on my creativity.
Creativity loves constraints.
There are few legal constraints on the sale of firearms in the U.S.
I think I've showed considerable constraint under the circumstances.
The cost of electricity is a chief constraint for Senegal's development.

etymology.text: From Middle English constreynt, constreynte, from Old French constreinte, past participle of constreindre (“to constrain”), from Latin cōnstringō (corresponding to the past participle cōnstrictus).

senses.definition: To define the scope of something.
To limit (an object or variable) to a certain region of program source code.
To perform a cursory investigation of; scope out.
To perform any medical procedure that ends in the suffix -scopy, such as endoscopy, colonoscopy, bronchoscopy, etc.
To examine under a microscope.
To observe a bird using a spotting scope.

If we locally scope the user's login name, it won't be accessible from outside this function.
The entomologist explained that he could not tell what species of springtail we were looking at without scoping it.

etymology.text: From Italian scopo (“purpose”), from Latin scopus (“target”), from Ancient Greek σκοπός (skopós), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ-. Etymologically related to skeptic and spectrum.

senses.definition: To evoke an intense interest or attraction in someone.
To make someone hold motionless; to spellbind.
To be irresistibly charming or attractive to.

examples.text: Slavic languages fascinate me.

examples.text: Mary was always fascinated by archaeology.
Young children are often fascinated by science.
examples.translation: 小孩常常對科學很有熱情。

examples.text: I was fascinated by her sweet voice.
examples.translation: 我被她甜美的聲線迷倒了。

examples.text: Tom is likely to still be fascinated by that.

examples.translation: 儘管迷上了英語，許多日本人甚至不設法學習它。

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin fascinātus, perfect passive participle of fascinō (“to enchant, bewitch, fascinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fascinum (“a phallus-shaped amulet worn around the neck in Ancient Rome; witchcraft”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), itself of obscure origin.

senses.definition: A legal agreement in which a borrower pledges real property as collateral for a loan used to purchase or refinance that property.
The state of being pledged.

examples.text: Tom works at a mortgage brokerage.

Who can explain to me what a mortgage credit is?
There has never been a mortgage crisis in Algeria.
With so many unemployed, many can't pay their mortgages.
I suffered from my mortgage loan.

etymology.text: From Middle English morgage and Middle French mortgage, from Anglo-Norman morgage, from Old French mort gage (“dead pledge”), after a translation of judicial Medieval Latin mortuum wadium, with wadium from Frankish *wadi (“wager, pledge”). Compare gage and also wage. So called because rents and profits from the land were owed to the lender for as long as the gage existed (comparable to interest on a loan today), as opposed to the living gage, in which rents and profits automatically reduced the

senses.definition: To take or experience pride in something; to be proud of it.

examples.text: Many parents take pride in their children.
examples.translation: 很多父母以自己的孩子為傲。

etymology.text: From Middle English pryde, pride, from Old English prȳde, prȳte (“pride”) (compare Old Norse prýði (“bravery, pomp”)), derivative of Old English prūd (“proud”). More at proud. The verb derives from the noun, at least since the 12th century.

senses.definition: Ability, skillfulness, especially skill in making plans and carrying them into execution; dexterity in managing affairs, adroitness, practical cunning; ingenuity in constructing, dexterity .
Cunning, art, skill, or dexterity applied to bad purposes; artifice; guile; subtlety; shrewdness as demonstrated by being skilled in deception .
Skill, skilfulness, art, especially the skill needed for a particular profession .

A branch of skilled work or trade, especially one requiring manual dexterity or artistic skill, but sometimes applied equally to any business, calling or profession; the skilled practice of a practical occupation .
A trade or profession as embodied in its practitioners collectively; the members of a trade or handicraft as a body; an association of these; a trade's union, guild, or ‘company’ .
A vehicle designed for navigation in or on water or air or through outer space .
Boats, especially of smaller size than ships. Historically primarily applied to vessels engaged in loading or unloading of other vessels, as lighters, hoys, and barges.
Those vessels attendant on a fleet, such as cutters, schooners, and gunboats, generally commanded by lieutenants.
A woman.
Implements used in catching fish, such as net, line, or hook. Modern use primarily in whaling, as in harpoons, hand-lances, etc. .
Strength; power; might; force .
Occult art, magic .
A work or product of art .
Handmade items, especially domestic or decorative objects; handicrafts .
A device, a means; a magical device, spell or enchantment .
Learning of the schools, scholarship; a branch of learning or knowledge, a science, especially one of the ‘seven liberal arts’ of the medieval universities .

examples.text: She focused on perfecting her craft.

examples.translation: 湯姆喝精釀啤酒。

examples.text: She earns a living from the craft of writing.
"What craft do you know?" the wizard asked the youth.

examples.translation: 俄羅斯正向敘利亞派遣戰艦、海軍陸戰隊和登陸艇坦克，並向伊朗派遣潛艦裝備。

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English craft (“strength, skill”), from Old English cræft (“strength, skill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz (“strength, power”); further origin obscure.

senses.definition: To make by hand and with much skill.
To construct, develop something (like a skilled craftsman).
To combine multiple items to form a new item, such as armour or medicine.

examples.text: Children often use construction paper to make crafts.
examples.translation: 孩子們常用彩紙製作手工藝品。

examples.translation: 這款木質皮夾由一整塊胡桃木製成。

examples.translation: 數千名工人和工匠辛勤工作了 22 年，才打造出這座令人驚嘆的白色大理石建築。

examples.text: We must hand down our craft to posterity.
The artisan crafted a complicated tool.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English craft (“strength, skill”), from Old English cræft (“strength, skill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz (“strength, power”); further origin obscure.

senses.definition: US spelling of humour.

examples.text: A little humor never hurt anyone.

Our teacher has a wonderful sense of humor.
examples.translation: 我們的老師非常有幽默感。

examples.text: I know you don't believe my story, but humor me for a minute and imagine it to be true.

senses.definition: To make or render precise; to specify.

examples.text: The surgeon carefully used the medical scissors to make a precise incision during the surgical procedure.

etymology.text: From Middle French précis, from Latin praecīsus, perfect passive participle of praecīdere, from prae- (“before, in front”) + caedere (“cut; strike”), cognate with hit. Related to incise. Doublet of précis.

senses.definition: Way, manner, or method.

examples.text: Religion is regarded by the common people as true, by the wise as false, and by the rulers as useful.
examples.translation: 宗教在一般人的眼中是真理，在智者的眼中是謊言，而在統治者的眼中則是一種工具。

examples.text: A wise and perceptive comment.

etymology.text: From Middle English wys, wyse, from Old English wīs (“wise”), from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz (“knowledgeable, wise”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing; knowledge”), from *weyd- (“to see”).

senses.definition: Concerning the relationships between the governments of countries.
Exhibiting diplomacy; exercising tact or courtesy; using discussion to avoid hard feelings, fights or arguments.
Describing a publication of a text which follows a single basic manuscript, but with variants in other manuscripts noted in the critical apparatus.

senses.definition: A theatrical work, combining drama, music, song and sometimes dance; usually, one sung-through, based on classical music and seen as more artistic and formalized than other forms of musical theater.
The score for such a work.
The genre of such works, the art of composing operas.
A building designed for the performance of such works; an opera house.
A company dedicated to performing such works.
Any showy, melodramatic or unrealistic production resembling an opera.

senses.definition: Just, only; no more than, pure and simple, neither more nor better than might be expected.
Pure, unalloyed .
Nothing less than; complete, downright .

examples.translation: 你不再只是一個孩子了。

A body of standing water, inclusive of lakes, ponds, and pools, especially any broad and shallow one.

etymology.text: From Middle English mere, mer, from Anglo-Norman meer, from Old French mier, from Latin merus (“pure, unmixed, undiluted”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to sparkle, gleam”).

senses.definition: Relating to literature.

Bookish.

examples.translation: 今天天氣很好，不下雨，是晴天，不冷不熱。

examples.translation: 明天天氣不好，不是晴天，要下雪，很冷。

senses.definition: To move on skis.
To travel over (a slope, etc.) on skis; to travel on skis at (a place), (especially as a sport).

examples.translation: 在這裡我們整年都能享受到滑雪的樂趣。

senses.definition: That which is silent; a time of silence.

A member of the Silent Generation.

senses.definition: Not followed by up: to provide (something) with support.

To put ashore.

The thirty-second Lenormand card.

examples.translation: 我沒有把英語直譯成日語。

senses.definition: To draw conclusions from examining; to assess; to appraise.

etymology.text: First use appears c. 1920, originally vitamine (1912), from Latin vīta (“life”) (see vital) + amine (see amino acids). Vitamine coined by Polish biochemist Casimir Funk after the initial discovery of aberic acid (thiamine), when it was thought that all such nutrients would be amines. The term had become ubiquitous by the time it was discovered that vitamin C, among others, had no amine component. In 1920, British biochemist Jack Drummond proposed that the final -e be dropped to deemphasize the a

The amount a sack holds; also, an archaic or historical measure of varying capacity, depending on commodity type and according to local usage; an old English measure of weight, usually of wool, equal to 13 stone (182 pounds), or in other sources, 26 stone (364 pounds).
The plunder and pillaging of a captured town or city.
Loot or booty obtained by pillage.

Any disposable bag.
Dismissal from employment, or discharge from a position.

A sack coat; a kind of coat worn by men, and extending from top to bottom without a cross seam.
A variety of light-colored dry wine from Spain or the Canary Islands; also, any strong white wine from southern Europe; sherry.

Alternatively, possibly of Indo-Aryan origin, as the word was formerly a reference to the coast of India, though this is doubtful as no positive etymon can be identified.

etymology.text: Probably from Ancient Greek ἱστός (histós, “mast”) + γράμμα (grámma), although it is sometimes claimed to have been derived from historical + diagram; coined in 1891 by English mathematician Karl Pearson.

senses.definition: To represent (data) as a histogram.

etymology.text: Probably from Ancient Greek ἱστός (histós, “mast”) + γράμμα (grámma), although it is sometimes claimed to have been derived from historical + diagram; coined in 1891 by English mathematician Karl Pearson.

senses.definition: The tangible end product; that which will be delivered.

examples.text: Due to inclement weather, we will be unable to provide our deliverables.
We packaged the deliverable, a program called FLOOD.EXE, in an installer file.
Under this contract the deliverables include both software and hardware.

etymology.text: From deliver + -able.

senses.definition: To charge (somebody) more money than the correct amount or to surpass a certain limit while charging a bill.
To continue to charge (an electrical device) beyond its capacity.
To charge (someone) with an inflated number or degree of legal charges (for example, charging them with a more serious crime than was committed); to upcharge.
To charge or load too heavily; to burden; to oppress.
To fill too full; to crowd.
To exaggerate.

examples.text: The salespeople often overcharge me.
Upon review it looks like I was overcharged for this.
I think I've been overcharged.
It was never our intention to overcharge you.
Ziri overcharged the battery in cycles.

October 22, 1706, Alexander Pope, letter to Mr. Walsh
Our language is naturally overcharged with consonants.

etymology.text: From Middle English overchargen, equivalent to over- + charge.

senses.definition: To invest again, give another investment.

examples.text: Reinvest the money in the business.
Chemical companies are waiting until everything dies down before reinvesting.
How much money have they reinvested in the community?

etymology.text: From re- + invest.

senses.definition: To release government control (of a business or industry) to private industry.
To render (a variable, etc.) private in scope.
To render a thought or an idea, private in scope.

examples.text: The factory was privatized.
Does Algeria need to privatize its public utilities?
Does Algeria need to privatize its state-owned companies?
Does Algeria need to privatize its government-owned enterprises?
Algeria needs to privatize its economy.
Algeria needs an ambitious program to privatize public utilities.

etymology.text: From private + -ize.

senses.definition: Synonym of proofreading.

examples.text: I'd like to have my essay proofread by a native speaker.

relations.native: 織布師用來整理布料的分叉工具

etymology.text: From proof + read.

senses.definition: Alternative form of stock market.
To lessen in price or estimated value; to lower the worth of.
To decline in value over time.
To belittle or disparage.

examples.text: Should the Algerian dinar be depreciated again?
The Algerian dinar has been hardly depreciating.
Does the Algerian dinar have to be depreciated again?
Algeria shouldn't depreciate its national currency.
The Moroccan dirham is rapidly depreciating in value.
Algeria's currency, the dinar, has greatly depreciated.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle English depreciaten, borrowed from Late Latin dēpretiātus / dēpreciātus, perfect passive participle of dēpretiō / dēpreciō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + pretium (“price”) + -ō.

senses.definition: A device which binds together sheets of paper by driving a thin metal staple through the sheets and simultaneously folding over the ends of the staple against the back surface of the paper.
Any device for stapling with (small or large) staples, including any office stapler, staple gun, or hammer tacker.
A dealer in staple goods.
One employed to sort wool according to its staple.

examples.text: Our stapler is out of staples.
I need to buy a stapler and some other office supplies.
"Where are you going?" "To get a stapler." "What's wrong with this one?" "It's out of staples."

etymology.text: From staple (verb) + -er.

senses.definition: Requiring a (specified) way of life, habitat, etc.
Indispensable; essential; necessary; obligatory; mandatory; unavoidably invoked.
Bound by oath, law or duty.

examples.text: In addition to being the obligate food source for monarch caterpillars, milkweeds also provide abundant nectar for the adult butterflies.
In some languages such signaling is optional, whereas in others it is obligate.

relations.native: 強制性的規定或必須遵守的要求
迫切的、必須的、至關重要的

etymology.text: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Latin obligātus, perfect passive participle of obligō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of oblige, taken through French.

senses.definition: An obligate organism.

etymology.text: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Latin obligātus, perfect passive participle of obligō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of oblige, taken through French.

senses.definition: To divide into tranches.

etymology.text: Unadapted borrowing from French tranche, form of trancher (“to cut, to slice”), from Old French trenchier (“cut, make a cut”), possibly from Vulgar Latin *trinicāre (“cut in three parts”). Doublet of traunch and trench.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a factor or factorial.
Of or pertaining to a factor, a kind of business agent.
Of or pertaining to a factory.

examples.text: Five factorial equals one hundred and twenty.
What's the value of zero factorial (0!)?
In reply, Lisa asked me to calculate 100 factorial in my head.
The gamma function is a generalization of the factorial function.

etymology.text: From factor + -ial.

senses.definition: Free; liberal; loose.
Relaxed; hence, cheerful, merry.
Able to be dissolved; soluble.
Not adhering; loose.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin solutus, past participle of solvo.

senses.definition: Any substance that is dissolved in a liquid solvent to create a solution.

examples.text: The solute is a calcium salt.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin solutus, past participle of solvo.

senses.definition: The process of altering the relative value of a currency or other standard of exchange.
A reassessment of the value or worth of something; a reappraisal or reevaluation.

The application of compound growth to the value of a pension benefit, specifically from the date of the member leaving the scheme (for example, moving to a different employer) to the date that the member starts receiving the benefit (typically retirement).

examples.text: After the soldiers raided her farm for supplies, she was forced to a revaluation of their benefit as protectors.

etymology.text: From re- + valuation.

senses.definition: One who speculates; an observer; a contemplator.
One who forms theories; a theorist.
One who speculates; as in investing, one who is willing to take volatile risks upon invested principal for the potential of substantial returns.
Synonym of field goal.

examples.text: There are no winners in wars, except the speculators.
Speculators invest in wars.
In the last few years, Ukrainian speculators have robbed the country.
These luxury apartments stay empty, only being bought and sold by speculators.
Some speculators take advantage of the ignorance and helplessness of old people.
An inexperienced stock speculator could easily let his business go to pot and lose his entire fortune.

etymology.text: From Latin speculātor (“spy, explorer, investigator”), from speculor (“to watch, to observe”) + -tor (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from specula (“watchtower”), from speciō (“to watch, to observe”), q.v. In some senses, an agent noun formed within English from speculate. Doublet of spectator.

senses.definition: A finite sequence of terms.
A single row in a relational database.
A set of comma-separated values passed to a program or operating system as a parameter to a function call.
A fixed-size container data type similar to a list that can hold different types of elements.

examples.text: Tuples are immutable in Python.
Both Python and Haskell have a tuple data type as well as a list data type.
Unlike lists, tuples are not formed by consing.

etymology.text: From the ending of the words quintuple, sextuple; from Latin -plus.

senses.definition: The state of being a proprietor; ownership.

etymology.text: From proprietor + -ship.

senses.definition: An undervaluation; a price or rate below the actual worth.

etymology.text: From under- + value.

senses.definition: The person responsible for handling the accounts on a ship, or for dealing with the passengers on a ship or aircraft.

examples.text: The purser acts as the crew's private merchant aboard the ship.
The purser welcomed the passengers aboard and checked their tickets with practiced efficiency.
As the ship's purser, Tom was responsible for handling all financial transactions on board.
Any questions about the handling of money on this ship need to be referred to the purser, not the captain.

etymology.text: From purse + -er.

senses.definition: A person who makes a deposit, especially a deposit of money in a bank.

etymology.text: From deposit + -or.

senses.definition: Alternative spelling of descendant.
The act of restating.
A second or subsequent statement.
Any of several treatises published by the American Law Institute in which a group of legal scholars within a field of law set forth the principles of that field of law based on legal precedents.

etymology.text: From re- + statement.

senses.definition: Alternative form of video conference.

examples.text: Villagers receive care from doctors at the hospital through videoconferencing.
I videoconferenced with the client this morning.

senses.definition: To cause to change from being concentrated at one point or site to being distributed across several.
To reduce the authority of (a governing body) by distributing that authority among several bodies.
To become decentralized.
To bring (a suspect) to the ground by use of directed force; to tackle.

examples.text: We have to decentralize France.
Should Algeria decentralize its power?
Algeria needs to decentralize planning.
Decentralized energy may make the widespread use of renewable energy a real possibility.
Effective public policy is not a simple matter of centralize or decentralize, subsidize or privatize, regulate or deregulate.
The government planned to decentralize power to local councils.

etymology.text: From de- + centralize.

senses.definition: To make familiar by use; to cause to accept; to habituate, familiarize, or inure.
To be wont.
To cohabit.

examples.text: He's accustomed to speaking to foreigners.
examples.translation: 他習慣和外國人說話。

examples.text: I'm accustomed to getting up early.
examples.translation: 我習慣早起。

examples.text: He's accustomed to traveling.
examples.translation: 他習慣了旅行。

examples.text: I'm not accustomed to walking long distances.
examples.translation: 我走不慣遠路。

examples.text: You will soon get accustomed to living here.
examples.translation: 你很快就會習慣住在這裡。

examples.text: The people here are accustomed to the cold.
examples.translation: 這裡的人習慣了寒冷。

etymology.text: The verb is from Middle English accustomen, from Old French acoustumer, acustumer (Modern French accoutumer) corresponding to a (“to, toward”) + custom. More at custom, costume.

senses.definition: US and Oxford British English standard spelling of randomise.

examples.text: Let's randomize the order of the images in the slideshow.
The purpose of shuffling is to randomize a deck of cards.
The teacher likes to randomize the seating every month so that the students get to sit next to new people.
She enjoyed the creative challenge of trying to randomize her writing.
Randomize the order of the numbers.

etymology.text: From random + -ize.

senses.definition: The act of vending or selling; a sale.
A member of a Balto-Finnic people who lived between the 12th to 16th centuries in the area around the town of Wenden (now Cēsis) in present-day north-central Latvia.
The letter Ꝩ/ꝩ, used in Old Norse, related to the rune wynn (ᚹ, whence also Latin-script Ƿ/ƿ) but with the bowl open at the top, like a y.
The total sales of coal from a colliery.

etymology.text: 17th century, likely a backformation from earlier vendible, vendee, vendor inspired by the underlying French vendre, from Old French vendre, from Latin vendere, from vēnum dāre (“to give (something for) sale”).

senses.definition: To develop industry; to become industrial.
To organize along industrial lines.

examples.text: Boumediene tried to industrialize Algeria.
Has Algeria begun to industrialize?
Algeria needs to industrialize.
The country was industrialized very quickly.
Algeria needs to become highly industrialized.
Northern Italy is rich and industrialized.

etymology.text: Borrowed from French industrialiser.

senses.definition: Old-fashioned, out of date; outdated.

etymology.text: From out- + date.

senses.definition: To make obsolete or out of date.
To become obsolete or out of date.
To date someone of a different racial group.

examples.text: All these traditions are monstrously outdated.
His methods are outdated.
Are USB drives outdated?
This type of Kabyle dress is really outdated.
Tom criticized outdated laws that are still on the books.
The computer was so outdated that it was good for nothing.

relations.native: 因大量使用而損壞且破舊

etymology.text: From out- + date.

Of art or other things: appealing to the tastes of an intellectual or sophisticated (sense 1.1) person; cerebral; also, cultured, elegant, refined.
Mixed with a foreign or inferior substance; not genuine or pure; adulterated, impure.
Of a thing: having its meaning changed in a deceptive or misleading way.

senses.definition: American and Oxford British spelling of annualise.

examples.text: When annualized, the quarterly gain represents a 4% growth.

etymology.text: From annual + -ize.

senses.definition: To go sightseeing; to visit places of interest in a city, town or geographical area.

examples.text: We went sightseeing in Hokkaido.
Pietro was doing sightseeing.
Australia is a great place for sightseeing.
Dirigibles are sometimes used for advertising and sightseeing.
By the way, did you have any spare time to go sightseeing while you were there?

etymology.text: Back-formation from sightseeing.

senses.definition: Synonym of repairer, a person who repairs things.

etymology.text: From repair + -person on the model of repairman.

senses.definition: To disown the authority of; to repudiate.
To withdraw authorization or permissions from.

examples.text: Use a password to protect your laptop from unauthorized access.
I don't want unauthorized pictures of me on people's social media.

etymology.text: From un- + authorize.
